meta.notes: Each rotation contains general objectives (rotation-wide) and topic/lecture-specific objectives. Category labels (Knowledge, History taking, Physical examination, Differential diagnosis, Investigations, Management, Communication, Attitude, etc.) are preserved as prefixes where present in the source. Timetables, logistics, case scenarios, pre-requisites and delivery-shell lines are excluded.

general_objectives: Develop competence in obtaining history and physical examination in perioperative cases.
Utilize clinical problem-solving skills to develop a diagnostic and therapeutic plan.

general_objectives: Upon successful completion of this course, the student will be able to appreciate mind-body interactions: the biological mediating mechanisms and developmental processes that define the individual's response to stress and link behavioral and social science factors to disease, disorder, and health outcomes.
Patient behavior: the psychological principles of behavioral change that influence both the acquisition and modification of risk behaviors.

Physician role and behavior: the attitudes, values, biases, and ethical principles that influence physician perception, judgement, and behavior; recognition of and utilization of social/community resources.
Physician-patient interactions: the ability to communicate & share decision-making.
Social and cultural issues in health care, cultural competence, and the impact of social inequities.
Health policy and economics: the health care system, economic barriers & incentives for physicians & patients.

Knowledge: Discuss the principles of family medicine: continuity of care, comprehensiveness, caring, coordination, clinical competence, cost-effectiveness, community, prevention and family.

Knowledge: Identify the role of the family medicine principles in both process and outcomes of care, such as prevention or reduction of physical, mental, and social disabilities, increased patient satisfaction and reduced aggregate healthcare spending.
Knowledge: Recognize the family physician role in understanding patients' social and family context.
Knowledge: Recognize the types of continuity of care: personal/relational; team; cross-boundary; informational; management.
Skills: Apply good communication skills that promote continuity when consulting patient.
Skills: Address the importance of continuity during consultation and encourage patients to maintain.

topics.title: Urinary tract infection (UTI)
objectives: Knowledge: Discuss the causes of dysuria & associated conditions in children - infectious causes: cystitis, pyelonephritis, urethritis, balanitis and balanoposthitis; noninfectious conditions: vesicoureteral reflux, urinary tract stones, irritants, trauma, labial adhesions, tumors.
Knowledge: Describe common causes of dysuria in women: cystitis/pyelonephritis/urinary tract stones; urethral syndrome; vaginitis; estrogen deficiency changes; genital herpes.
Knowledge: Describe common causes of dysuria in men: urethritis; cystitis/pyelonephritis/urinary tract stones; genital herpes; balanitis.
Knowledge: Discuss the signs and symptoms of the following: cystitis/pyelonephritis/urinary tract stones; prostatitis; urethritis; vaginitis; genital herpes; balanitis.
History-taking skills: Differentiate the typical presenting features of cystitis, pyelonephritis, and urethritis from each other.
History-taking skills: Define details of dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, and/or hematuria.
History-taking skills: Recognize the signs and symptoms of bacteremia and sepsis.

History-taking skills: Explain factors that may predispose a patient to cystitis, pyelonephritis, urethritis, and asymptomatic bacteriuria including: sexual activity; pregnancy; barrier contraceptives (diaphragm); prior urinary tract instrumentation; urinary catheterization (in-dwelling and intermittent); anatomic anomalies (congenital and acquired); bladder dysfunction.
Physical examination: Recognize the specific findings on physical examination that may suggest a particular underlying cause of dysuria in children (fever, extra-genital findings, genital findings).
Physical examination: In men, the physical examination should include lymph node palpation and inspection and palpation of the testicles, penis and prostate, digital rectal examination.
Physical examination: In women: fever, costovertebral angle tenderness, abdominal examination, pelvic examination if factors suggesting vaginitis or urethritis.

Investigations: Discuss and interpret the types of investigations for the diagnosis of urinary tract infection: urine dipstick and urinalysis; urine MCS (microscopy, culture & sensitivity); X-ray KUB; ultrasound KUB; CT KUB; swabs for microscopy and culture from the genital discharges/ulcers; voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG); radionuclide cystogram; renal cortical scan (DSMA scan); intravenous pyelogram.
Management: Discuss non-pharmacological management such as encouraging intake of sufficient fluid, personal hygiene, avoidance of local irritants and some drinks.
Management: Discuss the rationale for selecting a particular type of antimicrobial therapy for cystitis and pyelonephritis for specific duration.

Management: Recognize the commonly used antimicrobial drugs for urinary tract infections by naming drugs and the class to which each belongs, describing the antimicrobial spectrum for each and their effectiveness: amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, fosfomycin, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, ofloxacin.
Management: Summarize when to refer the patient to urologist/nephrologist for further evaluation and management.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Discuss the impact of the problem on the patient's life.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Show empathy and respect to the patient.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Explain the need to keep confidentiality and to be non-judgmental.

topics.title: Headache

Knowledge: Define the criteria for diagnosis of primary headaches as per the international classification of headache disorders.
Knowledge: Discuss an effective approach to patients presenting with medication induced headache.
Knowledge: Define chronic daily headache and discuss the common causes and its management.
Knowledge: Identify the common causes of secondary headaches and their typical symptoms and signs.
Knowledge: Discuss and describe indications for imaging in patients presenting with headache.
History-taking skills: Obtain comprehensive history in patients presenting with headache for the first time.
History-taking skills: Discuss focused history in patients known to have a primary headache disorder.
History-taking skills: Recognize red flags in patients presenting with headache.
Physical examination: Perform a proper neurological examination in patients presenting with headaches.
Physical examination: Perform a focused physical examination in patients presenting with symptoms suggestive of a secondary headache.
Management: Discuss an effective, and evidence-based management plan for patients presenting with primary headaches including preventive strategies.
Management: Describe the appropriate therapy for various types of headaches.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Discuss the importance of lifestyle changes in the management of primary headaches.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Respond to patient worries effectively.

topics.title: Hyperglycemia
objectives: Knowledge: Describe the types of diabetes mellitus (DM).
Knowledge: Define the pathogenesis, genetics, and epidemiology of DM.
Knowledge: Discuss the modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors for DM and methods used to prevent or delay the occurrence of DM.
Knowledge: Define impaired glucose tolerance (IGT) and impaired fasting glucose (IFG).

Knowledge: Explain the mechanism by which IFG and IGT translate, along with some other clinical parameters such as dyslipidemia, raised blood pressure and obesity, into a cardiovascular risk syndrome called the metabolic syndrome.
Knowledge: Define the diagnostic criteria for type II diabetes mellitus, based on history, physical examination and laboratory testing.

Knowledge: List the major causes of morbidity and mortality in type I and type II diabetes mellitus (e.g. coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, hypoglycemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, non-ketotic hyperglycemic coma, retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy, foot disorders).
Knowledge: Discuss the role of antidiabetic, lipid lowering and antihypertensive medications and their pharmacological actions.
Knowledge: Explore the up-to-date targets of treatment in diabetes (BP, lipids, weight, glucose).
History-taking skills: Elicit symptoms of diabetes and other relevant endocrinopathies, and recognize their role in identifying the type of DM.
History-taking skills: Elicit the other causes of DM like endocrinopathies, pancreatic tumors, radiation, etc.
History-taking skills: Elicit personal medical and surgical history with relevance to cardiometabolic disease.
History-taking skills: Elicit family history of diabetes and cardiometabolic risk factors (e.g. BP, lipids, obesity, and premature cardiovascular deaths).
History-taking skills: Explore occupational history with reference to issues such as stress and adjustment issues.
History-taking skills: Obtain relevant lifestyle history, e.g. diet, smoking, alcohol consumption, and physical activity.

Differential diagnosis: Propose differential diagnosis for abnormal blood lipids.
Investigations: Propose investigations for hyperglycemia e.g.: random versus fasting blood sugar, oral glucose tolerance test, glycated HbA1c.
Investigations: Propose investigations for abnormal blood lipids e.g.: lipid profile.
Investigations: Propose investigations for high blood pressure e.g.: ECG.
Investigations: Propose investigations for kidney function e.g.: urea & electrolytes and test for microalbuminuria, such as ACR.
Investigations: Propose investigations for feet e.g. sensation with monofilament and ankle/brachial ratio, Doppler investigation as indicated.
Investigations: Propose investigations for eyes e.g. fundoscopy with retinal imaging.
Management: Know the goals of treatment of diabetes mellitus (e.g., preventing complications, maintaining acceptable levels of glycemic control, and achieving weight reduction, if obese).
Management: Propose a management plan for hyperglycemia, e.g. use of anti-diabetic drugs such as oral hypoglycaemics and/or insulin.
Management: Propose a management plan for dyslipidemia and high blood pressure in line with respective objectives.
Management: Propose a management plan for microalbuminuria e.g. ACE inhibitors.
Management: Lifestyle modification with emphasis on diet, physical activity, such as exercise training, and smoking cessation.
Management: Consider low dose aspirin treatment as indicated for primary prevention.
Management: Propose a management plan for any underlying cause of diabetes.
Management: Describe the long-term treatment plan for diabetes.
Management: Include patients and families, as appropriate, in the development of treatment plans.
Management: Collaborate effectively with other members of the health care team, such as a nutritionist, nurse, or health educator.

Attitudes and professional behavior: Emphasize the importance of compliance and continuity of care to prevent complications.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Elicit history of high-risk behavior, such as indulgence in fatty foods, sedentary lifestyle, and smoking.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Appraise the benefit/risk ratio of anti-diabetic drug treatment.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Demonstrate skills in communication of risk to patients.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Demonstrate skills in risk modifying behavior counseling.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Address patient's ideas, concerns and expectations.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Discuss with patients and their families what the diagnosis of diabetes means, including the necessary lifestyle changes.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Demonstrate sensitivity and responsiveness with patients who are not adhering to treatment plans.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Reflect on personal frustrations when patients are not adherent to plans.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Explain the relationship of diabetes to culture, age, gender, and disabilities.

topics.title: Joint pain

Attitudes and professional behavior: Explain the diagnosis to the patient in clear simple language, avoiding medical jargon.

Knowledge: Differentiate between neuropathic versus nociceptive pain and identify the causes of each.
Knowledge: Assess the severity of pain by using the commonly used pain scales.
Knowledge: Know the impact of chronic pain on the overall well-being of patients, including health promotion and disease prevention.
Knowledge: Use best evidence to answer clinical questions about chronic pain.
Knowledge: Discuss appropriate investigations for each patient with low back pain, according to the differential diagnosis.
Knowledge: Explain the role of imaging and type of imaging in patients with low back pain.

Attitudes and professional behavior: Include patients and families in the development of treatment plans.
Attitudes and professional behavior: Demonstrate effective listening skills and empathy to improve patient adherence to lifestyle modifications (e.g., exercise, nutrition, and medications).

Knowledge: List common problems in advanced pregnancy.

Physical examination: Conduct a focused physical examination following travel, focusing on specific complaints.

Management: Discuss the common factors that affect personal safety and security.
Management: Give advice on common infectious diseases and how to avoid them.
Management: Provide advice about high altitude-related medical problems' prevention.
Management: Discuss the various vaccinations and prophylaxis and when they should be administered.
Management: Discuss the common medical problems commonly observed post travel.

Attitudes and professional behavior: Demonstrate understanding of common post-travel medical issues.

Knowledge: Know how to provide care to patients with previous history of bariatric surgery (post-bariatric care).

History-taking skills: Elicit family history of obesity.

History-taking skills: Determine which factors may precipitate dyspnoeic episodes in patients with asthma or chronic obstructive lung disease.

Physical examination: Perform a general physical examination and examination of the respiratory and cardiovascular systems to establish a diagnosis and identify the severity to aid in further evaluation and management.

Physical examination: In the event of an acute episode, focus the initial examination on assessing the severity of the condition: respiratory rate, levels of respiratory distress; identify signs of severe respiratory distress such as tachypnoea, tachycardia, cyanosis, respiratory muscle fatigue; identify acute severe asthma, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema by physical examination; distinguish the unilateral hyper-resonant note of pneumothorax from generalized hyper-resonance seen in emphysema; distinguish wheezes from crackles; identify and measure jugular venous pulse/pressure.
Physical examination: Identify clinically a cause for an acute episode keeping the differentials in mind.
Differential diagnosis: Generate differential diagnoses; identify whether the cause is acute or chronic; recognize whether it is a primary cardiac or respiratory event.

Differential diagnosis (acute dyspnoea, minutes to hours): Cardiac causes - ischemic heart disease (acute myocardial ischemia), myocardial dysfunction (congestive heart failure: ischemic/hypertensive cardiomyopathy, dilated cardiomyopathy - idiopathic, alcoholic, haemochromatosis), pericardial disease (tamponade and constrictive pericarditis). Pulmonary causes - upper airway (aspiration, anaphylaxis); ventilatory pump (pleura: pneumothorax; airways: bronchitis, bronchospasm); gas exchange (pulmonary embolus, pneumonia - viral, bacterial, atypical, fungus, ARDS, vasculitis - Wegener, Goodpasture); respiratory control (metabolic acidosis, salicylate toxicity).

Differential diagnosis (chronic dyspnoea, weeks to months): Differentiate acute from chronic dyspnoea; causes of shortness of breath include cardiopulmonary disorders, anemia, anxiety, neuromuscular problems, deconditioning, etc.
Laboratory interpretation: Interpret the arterial blood gas values.
Laboratory interpretation: Calculate A-a oxygen difference and use it to differentiate conditions with ventilation/perfusion disturbances from those with reduced alveolar ventilation.

Management: Make an accurate assessment of the severity of dyspnoea.

Management: Describe treatment options for dyspnoea including the mechanisms and potential adverse effects of these treatments and optimal treatment choices: oxygen; bronchodilators; antibiotics; diuretics; non-invasive ventilation; mechanical ventilation.

Management: Conduct an effective plan of management for a patient with chronic dyspnoea: discuss the chronic pharmacological management of patients with obstructive airways disease; discuss the management of cardiac failure; discuss the management of hypertension.
Management: Evaluate and manage patients presenting to casualty with acute shortness of breath.
Management: Management of acute severe asthma, pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism and pulmonary oedema.
Management: Select patients requiring hospitalization.
Management: Identify appropriate time for patient referral.
Behavior: Demonstrate commitment using risk-benefit, cost-benefit, and evidence-based considerations in the selection of diagnostic and therapeutic interventions for dyspnoea.
Behavior: Recognize the importance of patient preferences when selecting the diagnostic and therapeutic options for dyspnoea.
Behavior: Demonstrate ongoing commitment to self-directed learning regarding dyspnoea.
Behavior: Appreciate the impact of dyspnoea on a patient's quality of life, wellbeing, and ability to work and also the impact on the family.
Behavior: Recognize the importance of other healthcare professionals in the diagnosis and treatment of dyspnoea.
Behavior: Show understanding for the difficulties patients face with smoking cessation.

topics.title: Chest pain
objectives: Knowledge: Recognize the common causes of chest discomfort and differentiate cardiac pain from non-cardiac chest discomfort.
Knowledge: Understand the relevance of cardiac auscultatory findings in a patient with ischaemic heart disease.
Knowledge: Know the importance of risk factors in identifying ischaemic heart disease.
Knowledge: Learn to interpret the ECG in ischaemic heart disease.
Knowledge: Understand the pathophysiology of acute coronary syndromes and non-atherosclerotic causes of ischaemic chest pain.
History-taking skills: Elicit relevant history to differentiate cardiac and non-cardiac pain.
History-taking skills: Elicit relevant history of risk factors for coronary artery disease, modifiable and non-modifiable.
Physical exam skills: Learn and practice the general examination in identifying peripheral stigmata of atherosclerosis.
Physical exam skills: Identify auscultatory findings such as S3, S4 and murmurs precipitated by cardiac ischaemia.
Physical exam skills: Identify non-ischaemic causes of chest discomfort such as pericarditis, aortic dissection.
Physical exam skills: Describe the pathophysiological mechanisms of complications of myocardial ischemia such as heart failure and cardiac rupture.
Differential diagnosis: Propose a differential diagnosis of chest discomfort.
Differential diagnosis: Propose a differential diagnosis of cardiac chest discomfort.
Differential diagnosis: Propose a differential diagnosis of acute coronary syndromes.
Laboratory interpretation: Learn to order appropriate investigations in a patient with chest discomfort.
Laboratory interpretation: Know when to order ECG, CXR, echocardiography, treadmill testing and myocardial perfusion imaging and know the expected abnormalities.
Laboratory interpretation: Propose and justify the cardinal investigations in a patient suspected to have ischaemic heart disease such as biochemical markers of myocardial damage and lipids.
Laboratory interpretation: Propose appropriate investigations for detecting the coronary lesion such as cardiac CT and coronary angiography.
Communication skills: Communicate with the patient to explain the significance of chest discomfort.
Communication skills: Explain the possible cause of the chest discomfort and need for further investigations.
Management: Propose a management plan for acute coronary syndromes.
Management: Propose a management plan for chronic stable angina and secondary and primary prevention of ischaemic heart disease.
Behavior: Elicit history of high-risk cases for acute coronary syndromes.
Behavior: Explain the need for specialized treatment including percutaneous intervention and CABG.
Behavior: Obtain consent for physical examination and further investigations and treatment.

topics.title: Confusion / Delirium / Coma
objectives: Knowledge: Define the terms confusion and delirium.
Knowledge: Describe symptoms commonly associated with confusion/delirium.
Knowledge: List the common causes of confusion/delirium.
Knowledge: Describe pathophysiology of confusion/delirium due to common causes.
Knowledge: Define coma and describe clinical symptoms commonly associated.
Knowledge: List common causes of coma and describe pathophysiology and localization of lesions causing coma.
Knowledge: List common investigations considered in patients with confusion/delirium and coma.
Knowledge: List common predictors of poor outcome in confusion/delirium and coma.
Knowledge: List common measures for controlling agitated patients and describe their use.
History-taking skills: Obtain a focused history pertaining to confusion/delirium and coma, enabling recognition of associated symptoms and elucidation of possible cause(s).
Physical exam skills: Recognize signs in general physical examination pertinent to cause of confusion.
Physical exam skills: Evaluate consciousness using Glasgow Coma Score.

Physical exam skills: Perform a focused neurologic examination so as to document level of consciousness, associated behavioral and autonomic changes, presence of any focal neurologic and meningeal signs.
Physical exam skills: Perform a systemic examination so as to recognize signs of major organ dysfunction contributing to confusion/delirium.

Differential diagnosis: Generate a prioritized differential diagnosis of the causes of confusion/delirium and coma - systemic: intoxication/withdrawal (drugs: opiates, psychotropic, anticholinergic; withdrawal: alcohol, opiates; poisoning), metabolic (electrolyte disturbances - hyponatremia/hypernatremia, hypercalcemia; hypoglycemia; organ failure - hypoxemia, cardiac failure, uremia, hepatic encephalopathy, hypercarbia), miscellaneous (systemic sepsis, post-operative states, endocrinopathies); local (CNS): CNS infections, acute vascular events (stroke), trauma, neoplasm.

Laboratory interpretation: Recommend appropriate laboratory investigations and interpret them. Tests may include: CT brain/MRI brain; EEG; CSF analysis; tests to recognize common metabolic disorders/drug overdose/infections.
Procedural skills: Assess Glasgow Coma Score; objectively assess and describe patient behaviour in simple terms; describe indications for and method of performing lumbar puncture.
Communication skills: Explain to the patient's family the likely cause of delirium/confusion, plan of management and possible prognosis.
Management: Develop a management plan addressing: the underlying cause; the control of agitation and the minimizing of self-injury.
Behavior: Recognize that delirium is a serious threat to health and is associated with high mortality.
Behavior: Recognize causes/conditions requiring urgent treatment and ICU care.
Behavior: Recognize conditions associated with high mortality.

topics.title: Diabetes mellitus
objectives: Knowledge: Diagnostic criteria for impaired fasting glucose and impaired glucose tolerance.
Knowledge: Diagnostic criteria for type I and type II diabetes mellitus, based on history, physical examination, and laboratory testing.
Knowledge: Pathophysiology, risk factors, and epidemiology of type I and type II diabetes mellitus.
Knowledge: The basic principles of the role of genetics in diabetes mellitus.
Knowledge: Presenting symptoms and signs of type I and type II diabetes mellitus.
Knowledge: Presenting symptoms and signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and nonketotic hyperglycemia (NKH).
Knowledge: Pathophysiology for the abnormal laboratory values in DKA and NKH including plasma sodium, potassium, and bicarbonate.
Knowledge: Precipitants of DKA and NKH.

Knowledge: Major causes of morbidity and mortality in diabetes mellitus (coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, hypoglycemia, DKA, NKH coma, retinopathy, neuropathy - peripheral and autonomic, nephropathy, foot disorders, infections).

Knowledge: Laboratory tests needed to screen, diagnose, and follow diabetic patients including: glucose, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen/creatinine, fasting lipid profile, HbA1c, urine microalbumin/creatinine ratio, urine dipstick for protein.

Knowledge: Non-pharmacologic and pharmacologic (drugs and side effects) treatment of diabetes mellitus to maintain acceptable levels of glycemic control, prevent target organ disease, and other associated complications.
Knowledge: The specific components of the American Diabetes Association (ADA) dietary recommendations for type I and type II diabetes mellitus.
Knowledge: Basic management of diabetic ketoacidosis and nonketotic hyperglycemic states, including the similarities and differences in fluid and electrolyte replacement.
Knowledge: Basic management of blood glucoses in the hospitalized patient.
Knowledge: The Somogyi effect and the Dawn phenomenon and the implications of each in diabetes.
Knowledge: Pharmacologic management of diabetes mellitus.
Knowledge: The fundamental aspects of the American Diabetes Association (ADA) clinical practice recommendations and how they encourage high quality diabetes care.
Knowledge: Basic management of hypertension and hyperlipidemia in the diabetic patient.

History-taking skills: Obtain, document, and present an age-appropriate medical history that differentiates among etiologies of disease, including: weight changes; hypo- or hyperglycemic symptoms; medication history (adherence, side effects, other medications); home glucose monitoring results; target organ disease complications (cardiovascular, foot, gastrointestinal, infectious, neurological, sexual, skin, urinary, or vision symptoms); diet history (total caloric intake, intake of sugar-containing foods, intake of saturated fat and cholesterol, physical activity level, timing of meals).

Physical exam skills: Perform a physical exam to establish the diagnosis and severity of disease, including: skin examination for diabetic dermopathy, furuncles/carbuncles, candidiasis, necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum, dermatophytosis, and acanthosis nigricans; fundoscopic exam; arterial pulses; peripheral nerves (e.g. monofilament testing); examination of the feet for corns, calluses, and ulcerations; in patients with DKA or NKH evaluate for mental status alterations, Kussmaul's respirations, fruity breath, and signs of volume depletion.

Differential diagnosis: Generate a prioritized differential diagnosis recognizing specific history and physical exam findings that suggest a specific etiology for: hyperglycemia; hypoglycemia; anion gap acidosis; ketosis; hyperosmolality.

Laboratory interpretation: Recommend when to order diagnostic and laboratory tests and interpret them, both prior to and after initiating treatment, based on the differential diagnosis, including consideration of test cost and performance characteristics as well as patient preferences. Tests should include, when appropriate: fasting serum glucose; electrolytes, BUN/Cr; serum and urine ketones; serum and urine osmolality; HbA1c; fasting lipid profile; urinalysis; urine microalbumin/creatinine ratio; 24-hour urine for protein and creatinine clearance.

Communication skills: Communicate the diagnosis, treatment plan, and subsequent follow-up to patients; elicit questions from the patient and their family about the management plan; counsel patients appropriately on dietary measures, exercise, medication adherence, proper foot care, and prevention of other target organ disease.
Procedural skills: Finger-stick capillary blood glucose determination; obtain an ABG.
Management: Ability to perform a complete medical history and physical examination.
Management: Write appropriate fluid and insulin orders and outline critical steps for the treatment of DKA and NKH.
Management: Counsel patients regarding basic features of ADA diabetic diet recommendations.
Management: Instruct patients in home blood glucose monitoring.

Management: Counsel patients on behavior changes (smoking cessation, medication adherence, poor glycemic control, obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and infection) to avoid the complications of diabetes.
Management: Counsel patients regarding basic foot care.
Management: Determine when to institute diet therapy, oral hypoglycemic agents, and insulin therapy.
Management: Calculate an appropriate insulin dose for a diabetic patient.
Management: Use community resources (hospital and community-based education programs) to aid the patient in understanding and managing his or her illness.
Management: Determine when to obtain consultation from an endocrinologist, nephrologist, ophthalmologist, podiatrist, and dietician.
Management: Access and utilize appropriate information systems and resources to help delineate issues related to diabetes mellitus.
Management: Incorporate patient preferences.
Behavior: Demonstrate commitment to using risk-benefit, cost-benefit, and evidence-based considerations in the selection of diagnostic and therapeutic interventions for diabetes mellitus.
Behavior: Recognize the importance of patient preferences when selecting among diagnostic and therapeutic options for diabetes mellitus.
Behavior: Respond appropriately to patients who are nonadherent to treatment for diabetes mellitus.
Behavior: Demonstrate ongoing commitment to self-directed learning regarding diabetes mellitus.
Behavior: Appreciate the impact diabetes mellitus has on a patient's quality of life, wellbeing, ability to work, and the family.
Behavior: Recognize the importance of and demonstrate a commitment to the utilization of other healthcare professionals in the treatment of diabetes mellitus.

topics.title: Edema
objectives: Knowledge: Differentiate transudate and exudates.
Knowledge: Differentiate clinical syndromes associated with oedema (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, etc.).
Knowledge: Describe clinical features of pulmonary oedema.
Knowledge: Explain the procedure of abdominal paracentesis, with indications and complications.
Knowledge: Explain the procedure of thoracocentesis, with indications and complications.
Skills: Demonstrate relevant history taking skills to identify risk factors for development of oedema and to determine the extent and severity of oedema.
Skills: Demonstrate clinical examination skills to assess localization and severity of oedema.
Skills: Describe chest x-ray findings of pulmonary oedema.
Skills: Suggest relevant laboratory investigations appropriate for the clinical syndrome leading to oedema.
Skills: Describe the interpretation of laboratory findings relevant for the clinical syndrome leading to oedema.
Management: List non-pharmacological (diet, fluid intake) and pharmacological options of treatment of peripheral oedema and pulmonary oedema.
Management: Detail non-pharmacological management of oedema.
Management: Detail pharmacological management of oedema.
Management: Describe/recognize side effects of the pharmacological management of oedema.

topics.title: Electrolyte abnormalities
objectives: Knowledge: The pathophysiology of: hypo- and hypervolaemia; hypo- and hypernatraemia; hypo- and hyperkalaemia; hypo- and hypercalcaemia; simple and mixed acid-base disorders; respiratory acidosis and alkalosis; metabolic acidosis and alkalosis.
Knowledge: Presenting symptoms and signs of the above disorders.
Knowledge: The importance of total body water and its distribution.
Knowledge: The differential diagnosis of hypo- and hypernatraemia in the setting of volume depletion, euvolaemia, and hypervolaemia.
Knowledge: How to distinguish hyponatraemia from pseudohyponatraemia.
Knowledge: How to identify spurious hyperkalaemia and acidosis-related hyperkalaemia.
Knowledge: Risks of too rapid or delayed therapy for hyponatraemia.
Knowledge: The most common causes of respiratory acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis.
Knowledge: How to calculate the anion gap and explain its relevance to determining the cause of a metabolic acidosis.
Knowledge: Changes in total body water distribution that occur with aging.
Knowledge: How altered mental status can contribute to electrolyte disorders.
Knowledge: Tests to use in the evaluation of fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base disorders.
Knowledge: Indications for obtaining ABGs.
Knowledge: The types of fluid preparations to use in the treatment of fluid and electrolyte disorders.

History-taking skills: Elicit appropriate information from patients with volume overload, including recent weight gain, oedema or ascites, symptoms of heart failure, dietary sodium intake, changes in medications, noncompliance and intravenous fluid regimens.

History-taking skills: Elicit appropriate information from patients with volume depletion, including recent weight loss, thirst, gastrointestinal losses, urinary losses, oral intake, insensible losses, and intravenous fluid regimens.

History-taking skills: Elicit appropriate information from patients with electrolyte problems, including use of diuretics and other medications, gastrointestinal losses, and history of relevant medical conditions (e.g., heart failure, liver disease, renal disease, pulmonary disease, CNS disease, and malignancy).
Physical exam skills: Measurement of orthostatic vital signs.
Physical exam skills: Identification of signs of volume overload including peripheral oedema, pulmonary oedema, pleural effusions and ascites.

Physical exam skills: Identification of signs of volume depletion including tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor and a low or undetectable jugular venous pressure.
Physical exam skills: Identification of signs of sodium disorders including lethargy, weakness, encephalopathy, delirium, seizures.

Physical exam skills: Identification of signs of potassium disorders including weakness, fatigue, constipation, ileus, cramping, tetany, hypo- or hyperreflexia, and cardiac arrhythmias including cardiac arrest.

Physical exam skills: Identification of signs of calcium disorders including cramping, tetany, Chvostek's and Trousseau's sign, seizures, anorexia, constipation, polyuria, hypo- or hyperreflexia, stupor, coma.

Differential diagnosis: Generate a prioritized differential diagnosis recognizing specific history, physical exam, and laboratory findings that distinguish between: hypo- and hypervolaemia; hypo- and hypernatraemia; hypo- and hyperkalaemia; hypo- and hypercalcaemia; respiratory acidosis and alkalosis; metabolic acidosis and alkalosis.

Laboratory interpretation: Recommend when to order diagnostic and laboratory tests and interpret them, including: serum electrolytes, urea/creatinine; anion gap; ABGs; serum and urine osmolality; urinary sodium; fractional excretion of sodium; ECG findings in hyper- and hypokalemia; estimation of the osmolar gap.

Communication skills: Explain to a patient and his or her family why intravenous fluids are needed; communicate the diagnosis, treatment plan, and subsequent follow-up; elicit input and questions from the patient and their family about the management plan.
Procedural skills: Insert a peripheral intravenous catheter; obtain ABGs; assist in the insertion of a central venous catheter.

Management: Write appropriate fluid orders for the treatment of hypo- and hypervolaemia, hypo- and hypernatraemia, hypo- and hyperkalaemia, hypo- and hypercalcaemia; write appropriate orders for replacing sodium, potassium, and calcium.
Management: Write appropriate orders for managing hyperkalaemia and hypercalcaemia.
Management: Calculate the water deficit that needs to be corrected to treat hypernatraemia.
Management: Identify indications for administration of bicarbonate.
Management: Determine when to obtain consultation from a nephrologist.
Management: Use a cost-effective approach based on the differential diagnosis.
Management: Access and utilize appropriate information systems and resources to help delineate issues related to fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base disorders.
Management: Incorporate patient preferences.

Behavior: Demonstrate commitment to using risk-benefit, cost-benefit, and evidence-based considerations in the selection of diagnostic and therapeutic interventions for problems related to fluid, electrolyte and acid-base disorders.
Behavior: Demonstrate ongoing commitment to self-directed learning regarding fluid, electrolyte and acid-base disorders.
Behavior: Recognize the importance and demonstrate a commitment to the utilization of other healthcare professions in the treatment of problems related to fluid, electrolyte and acid-base disorders.

topics.title: Fever
objectives: Knowledge: Define fever and hypothermia.
Knowledge: Describe the criteria for fever of unknown origin.
Knowledge: Describe common infectious etiologies manifesting with prolonged fever and their epidemiology.
Knowledge: Explain the basic principles of investigations of a febrile patient.
Knowledge: List common non-infectious causes of fever (by category with examples).
Knowledge: Recognize fever in a traveler and list epidemiologically relevant infectious causes.
Knowledge: Develop an approach for work up of fever.
Knowledge: Develop an approach to management of a febrile patient.
Knowledge: Recognize serious infectious febrile syndromes associated with skin rash.

History-taking skills: Obtain, document, and present appropriate medical history that differentiates among etiologies of fever including: exposure history; occupational history; travel history; immunization and vaccination history.

Physical exam skills: Perform a physical exam to establish the underlying etiology of fever including: detailed examination of the oral cavity, ears and sinuses; examination of the lymph nodes; examination of the skin for rashes and specific lesions; examination of the abdomen with focus on liver and spleen; detailed cardiovascular examination for murmurs; examination of the respiratory system; examination of the central nervous system.

Differential diagnosis: Generate a prioritized differential diagnosis recognizing specific history and physical exam findings that suggest a specific etiology for the fever: malaria; endocarditis; tuberculosis; brucellosis; Q fever; noninfectious causes.

Laboratory interpretation: Know when to order diagnostic and laboratory tests and interpret them, including: full blood count, ESR and CRP; blood film for malaria; blood cultures and cultures from other sites as appropriate; specific serological and molecular tests as appropriate; chest x-ray; advanced radiology such as PET-CT in selected undifferentiated fever syndromes; echocardiography.
Communication skills: Communicate the diagnosis, treatment plan, and subsequent follow-up to patients; learn how to engage patient and their family about the management plan.
Procedural skills: Perform gram stain on a clinical specimen as indicated (urine/sputum); urinalysis and urine microscopy.

Management: Ability to perform a complete medical history and physical examination; write appropriate and focused investigations for a febrile patient; prescribe appropriate antimicrobials when indicated; counsel patients regarding procedures such as lumbar puncture; promote vaccination for vaccine-preventable diseases; use community resources to aid patients in the avoidance of potential infectious exposures; determine when to obtain consultations from public health officials.
Behavior: Demonstrate commitment to using risk-benefit, cost-benefit, and evidence-based considerations in the selection of diagnostic and therapeutic interventions.
Behavior: Recognize the importance of patient preferences when selecting diagnostic and therapeutic options.
Behavior: Recognize the importance of public health in the control of communicable diseases and the duty of the physician to report notifiable diseases.

topics.title: Gastrointestinal bleeding
objectives: Knowledge: The common causes for and symptoms of upper and lower gastrointestinal blood loss, including: esophagitis/esophageal erosions; Mallory-Weiss tear; peptic and duodenal ulcer disease; esophageal/gastric varices; erosive gastritis; arteriovenous malformations; gastrointestinal tumors, benign and malignant; diverticulosis; ischemic colitis; hemorrhoids; anal fissures.
Knowledge: The distinguishing features of upper versus lower GI bleeding.
Knowledge: The indications for inpatient versus outpatient evaluation and treatment.
Knowledge: The principles of stabilization and treatment of acute massive GI blood loss.
Knowledge: The role of contributing factors in GI bleeding such as H. pylori infection; NSAIDs, alcohol, cigarette use, coagulopathies; and chronic liver disease.

History-taking skills: Obtain, document, and present an age-appropriate history that differentiates among etiologies of disease, including: features that distinguish upper from lower GI bleeding; quantification of degree of blood loss; chronology and duration of bleeding; associated symptoms; relevant past medical history; medication history, including use of tobacco and alcohol.

Physical exam skills: Perform a physical examination to establish the diagnosis and severity of disease, including: postural blood pressure and pulse; abdominal palpation for organomegaly, masses, and tenderness; search for stigmata of chronic liver disease; anal and rectal examination.
Differential diagnosis: Generate a differential diagnosis; recognize specific history and physical examination findings that suggest a specific etiology for GI bleeding.

Laboratory interpretation: Recommend when to order diagnostic and laboratory tests and interpret them. Tests should include, when appropriate: stool and gastric fluid tests for occult blood; CBC; PT/PTT; LFT; tests for Helicobacter pylori. Define the indications for and interpret (with consultation) results of: esophagogastroduodenoscopy; colonoscopy; barium studies of the gastrointestinal tract.
Communication skills: Communicate the diagnosis, treatment plan, and subsequent follow-up to patients; elicit questions from the patient and his or her family about the management plan.

Management: Use a cost-effective approach based on the differential diagnosis; outline long-term management when appropriate (e.g. Helicobacter pylori eradication, antacid, H-2 blocker or proton pump inhibitor therapy, smoking/alcohol cessation, NSAID restriction, and dietary modification).
Behavior: Respond appropriately to patients who are nonadherent to treatment for gastrointestinal bleeding.
Behavior: Demonstrate ongoing commitment to self-directed learning.
Behavior: Appreciate the impact gastrointestinal bleeding has on a patient's quality of life, well-being, ability to work, and the family.

topics.title: Hemiplegia / Hemisensory loss +/- Aphasia
objectives: Knowledge: Define the terms hemiplegia, hemisensory loss (and aphasia).
Knowledge: Describe symptoms commonly associated with hemiplegia/hemisensory loss.
Knowledge: List common causes of hemiplegia/hemisensory loss (and similar focal neurologic syndromes).
Knowledge: List common investigations considered in patients with hemiplegia/hemisensory loss/focal neurologic syndromes.
Knowledge: List risk factors associated with cerebrovascular disorders.
Knowledge: Describe management of acute stroke.

Knowledge: Recognize the indications and contra-indications for intravenous and intra-arterial thrombolysis for acute stroke; describe benefits and complications associated with intravenous thrombolysis with tPA; and list minimum investigations prior to thrombolysis.
Knowledge: Explain to patient's relatives the essentials of caring for a patient with hemiplegia at home.
Knowledge: Describe long-term preventive measures for patients with stroke.
Knowledge: Describe management of an acute attack of multiple sclerosis.
Knowledge: Describe methods of preventing relapses in a patient with other causes of hemiplegia/hemisensory loss/focal neurologic syndromes.
History-taking skills: Obtain a focused history pertaining to hemiplegia/hemisensory loss/focal neurologic syndromes, enabling recognition of possible cause(s), risk factors and associated symptoms.
Physical exam skills: Recognize signs in general physical and systemic examination pertinent to risk factors and complications.
Physical exam skills: Perform a focused neurologic examination so as to document the severity and extent of weakness/sensory change.

Differential diagnosis: Analyze clinical signs and symptoms to arrive at a possible level of involvement in the neuraxis; analyze course of clinical events to generate a possible etiologic diagnosis; generate a prioritized differential diagnosis - acute hemiplegia (ischemic stroke - embolic, thrombotic; hemorrhagic stroke - epidural hemorrhage, intracerebral hemorrhage, subarachnoid hemorrhage; inflammatory causes - multiple sclerosis, sarcoidosis); subacute hemiplegia (subdural hematoma, infectious cause, primary CNS malignancy such as astrocytoma, metastases); chronic hemiparesis (benign neoplasm such as meningioma, unruptured compressive AVM, subdural hematoma); complications of hemiplegia (acute: pressure sores, deep vein thrombosis; chronic: contractures, spasms/spasticity, musculoskeletal pain, depression).

Laboratory interpretation: Recommend appropriate laboratory investigations and interpret them. Tests may include: imaging (CT brain/MRI brain or spine as appropriate); MR or CT angiography/digital subtraction angiography; CSF analysis; cardiovascular investigations; evoked potentials; tests to recognize common systemic disorders causing hemiplegia/hemisensory loss/focal neurologic syndromes.

Communication skills: Explain to a patient with acute stroke the possible benefits and risks associated with thrombolysis within the recognized time window; explain to a patient with a cerebrovascular disorder the role of possible risk factors and long-term measures aimed at secondary prevention; explain to a patient with other causes of hemiplegia/hemisensory loss/focal neurologic syndromes measures aimed at prevention of recurrence and of complications.
Behavior: Recognize high incidence of stroke and high associated mortality.
Behavior: Recognize that acute stroke is treatable within limited time-windows.
Behavior: Recognize that prevention of stroke is possible by effectively addressing common risk factors.
Behavior: Recognize that prevention of complications is possible in patients with residual neurologic deficits.

topics.title: Haemoptysis
objectives: Knowledge: Define haemoptysis including minimal, moderate and massive haemoptysis.
Knowledge: Differentiate between haemoptysis and haematemesis.
Knowledge: List and interpret critical clinical and laboratory findings which are key in the processes of exclusion, differentiation, and diagnosis.
Knowledge: Select investigations to determine the cause of haemoptysis (urinalysis, creatinine, liver function, coagulation tests, x-ray, CT scan).
Knowledge: List indications for bronchoscopy.

History taking skills: Determine whether the symptom is haemoptysis or haematemesis; categorize haemoptysis into minimal, moderate or life-threatening haemoptysis; differentiate between the causes of haemoptysis; determine the presence of prior lung, renal, or cardiac involvement and history of smoking; prior history of haemoptysis, infectious symptoms, upper airway or gastrointestinal symptoms; determine exposure to chemicals/asbestos, travel history, anticoagulants/antiplatelet drugs.

Physical exam skills: Categorize haemoptysis into minimal, moderate or life-threatening haemoptysis; look for vital signs - pulse, blood pressure, and SaO2; examine for skin rash, deep venous thrombi; good physical examination of the respiratory and cardiovascular system.

Differential diagnosis: Recognize the common causes - airway disease, the most common source of haemoptysis (inflammatory: bronchitis acute/chronic, bronchiectasis, lung abscess, cystic fibrosis; neoplastic: bronchogenic carcinoma, endobronchial metastatic carcinoma - breast, renal, colon, bronchial carcinoid, Kaposi sarcoma in patients with AIDS; other: foreign body, trauma); pulmonary parenchymal disease (infectious: TB, necrotizing pneumonia, mycetoma, aspergilloma; inflammatory/immune: Goodpasture, hemosiderosis, Wegener, lupus; other: coagulopathy, iatrogenic, cocaine, endometriosis); cardiac/vascular (pulmonary embolus with infarction, AV malformation; elevated capillary pressure - mitral stenosis, LV failure).

Laboratory interpretation: List and interpret critical clinical and laboratory findings; select investigations to determine the cause of haemoptysis: urinalysis; creatinine; liver function; coagulation tests; x-ray; CT scan; bronchoscopy; anti-nuclear antibody (ANA); anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA).
Communication skills: Reassure the patient on admission regarding treatment as haemoptysis is often an alarming symptom; discuss the need for bronchoscopy and obtain consent.
Procedural skills: Learn the basics of airway care; learn the process of Basic and Advanced Life Support activities.
Management: Conduct an effective initial plan of management for a patient with haemoptysis.

Management: In the presence of massive haemoptysis (>400 ml/day): ensure adequacy of ventilation and haemodynamic stability first and consult a specialist; attend to the care of the airway to prevent asphyxia; reverse coagulation disorders rapidly; identify the need for blood transfusion; identify the indications for bronchoscopy; recognize the indications for bronchial artery embolisation; outline the specific treatment for pulmonary renal syndromes or vasculitis.
Management: Triage and outline the management of causes of haemoptysis which are not life-threatening and do not require immediate referral to a specialist.
Management: Select patients in need of specialized care and/or consultation.
Behavior: Appreciate the extreme anxiety and the sense of impending doom on the part of a patient with massive hemoptysis.

topics.title: Hypoxia / Cyanosis
objectives: Knowledge: Define cyanosis, hypoxaemia, and hypoxia.
Knowledge: List the differential diagnoses for both acute and chronic hypoxia and differentiate between the major causes.

Knowledge: Differentiate between cyanosis of central origin (blood travelling in the aorta is already desaturated) and cyanosis of peripheral origin (local inadequacy of blood flow with stagnation and excessive oxygen extraction in the capillaries).
Knowledge: Outline the principles of appropriate management of hypoxia and reasons for specialist referral.
Knowledge: Identify potentially serious complications of hypoxia.
History taking skills: Obtain, document and present history working up at the same time a list of differential diagnoses; distinguish primary respiratory disorders from cyanotic heart disease(s).

Physical exam skills: Perform a focused general physical examination and identify cyanosis and clubbing; perform an examination of the respiratory and cardiovascular systems focusing on the likely causes; recognize the severity of the condition; differentiate between cyanosis of central origin and cyanosis of peripheral origin.

Differential diagnosis: Distinguish primary respiratory from cardiovascular disorder; identify whether the cause is acute or chronic; identify the different causes of central cyanosis and recognize the signs and symptoms of each (cardiac causes: right-to-left shunt; pulmonary causes: failure of oxygenation in the pulmonary capillaries); identify the different causes of peripheral cyanosis.

Laboratory interpretation: Interpret arterial (and venous) blood gas values; calculate A-a oxygen difference and use it to differentiate conditions with ventilation-perfusion disturbances from those with a normal A-a oxygen difference and hypoventilation; interpret other diagnostic and laboratory tests as appropriate: chest X-ray; chest CT; V/Q scan; CT angiogram; pulmonary function tests; ECG; ANA; ENA.

Communication skills: Counsel and educate patients about domiciliary oxygen therapy; discuss the ease of using oxygen concentrators; discuss the need and use of non-invasive ventilation using CPAP at home; discuss with the parents the diagnosis in congenital cyanotic heart diseases.

Procedural skills: Perform ABGs and ECG; identify the different types of oxygen delivery systems (nasal prongs, simple mask, non-rebreather mask, Venturi mask, etc.) and be able to connect each of these in different patients with hypoxia.

Management: Describe treatment options for hypoxia including the mechanisms and potential adverse effects of these treatments and optimal treatment choices - specifically: oxygen therapy (prescription, dose, delivery devices); non-invasive ventilation; ventilatory support.
Management: Identify the appropriate time for referral.
Management: Conduct an effective initial plan of management for a patient with hypoxaemia/cyanosis/hypoxia.
Management: Outline an initial plan of management which includes treatment of the underlying condition along with oxygen administration.
Management: Be familiar with oxygen concentrators.
Management: Explain the principles of long-term oxygen therapy.

topics.title: Hepatomegaly
objectives: Knowledge: The properties of the normal liver (size, location, consistency, anatomy, anatomic variations including Riedel's lobe and caudate lobe papillary process).

Knowledge: The epidemiology, pathophysiologic manifestations, symptoms, signs, and typical clinical course of tender and non-tender hepatomegaly - tender hepatomegaly: infection/inflammation (acute viral hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis), congestion (Budd-Chiari syndrome, right heart failure, hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome); non-tender hepatomegaly: obstruction of biliary system (cholestatic liver disease, gallstones), storage disorders (glycogen storage disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, hereditary hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease), infiltration (steatosis - alcoholic and non-alcoholic, primary or metastatic liver lesions).
Knowledge: The indications for and risks of liver biopsy.

Knowledge: The indications for and utility of hepatobiliary imaging studies, including: ultrasound; nuclear medicine studies; CT; MRI; magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP); endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).

Knowledge: Genetic considerations in liver disease (i.e. hemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, Gilbert's syndrome).
Knowledge: The epidemiology, pathophysiology, symptoms, signs, and typical clinical course of cholelithiasis and cholecystitis.
Knowledge: The clinical syndrome of 'ascending cholangitis' including its common causes and typical clinical course.
Knowledge: The indications for and risks of paracentesis and liver biopsy.
Knowledge: The indications for and utility of hepatobiliary imaging studies, including: ultrasound; nuclear medicine studies; CT; MRI; MRCP; ERCP.

Management: The diagnostic evaluation of patients with jaundice and unconjugated or conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Knowledge: Know the important causes of systolic and diastolic murmurs.
Knowledge: Learn the auscultatory signs of common cardiac valvular lesions.
Knowledge: Have knowledge of common congenital cardiac lesions in the adult age group.
History-taking skills: Elicit relevant history to suggest any previous rheumatic fever.
History-taking skills: Recognize the importance of suspecting infective endocarditis in a patient with fever and heart murmur and be able to take a relevant history.
Physical exam skills: Learn and practice the auscultation of the precordium and the classic areas of auscultation, including the areas of radiation of different murmurs.
Physical exam skills: Perform the different manoeuvres for eliciting the mitral murmurs in the mitral area and the aortic murmurs in the aortic area.
Physical exam skills: Elicit the diagnostic murmur of each cardiac valvular and congenital lesion in adults.

Physical exam skills: Understand the variation in murmurs to different phases of respiration and the significance of change in murmurs in response to other manoeuvres like squatting and Valsalva manoeuvre.
Physical exam skills: Differentiate murmurs from other added sounds which may mimic them, such as a pericardial friction rub.
Differential diagnosis: Propose a differential diagnosis of systolic murmurs; propose a differential diagnosis of diastolic murmurs.
Laboratory interpretation: Learn to order appropriate investigations in a patient with heart murmur.
Laboratory interpretation: Propose ECG, CXR and echocardiography and know the expected abnormalities.

Laboratory interpretation: Propose and justify the cardinal investigations in a patient suspected to have infective endocarditis such as blood cultures, CBC, ESR, urine microscopy, transthoracic and transesophageal echo to look for vegetations.
Laboratory interpretation: Propose appropriate investigations for acute rheumatic fever such as CBC, ESR, CRP, blood cultures, ASO titre, throat swab, etc.

Communication skills: Communicate with the patient to explain the significance of the murmur detected; explain the possible cause of the murmur and need for further investigations like echocardiography.
Procedural skills: Perform a 12-lead ECG.
Management: Propose a management plan for infective endocarditis; propose a management plan for acute rheumatic fever and acute carditis.
Behavior: Elicit history of high-risk cases for endocarditis, such as intravenous drug addicts, immunosuppressed patients e.g. HIV and those on chemotherapy.
Behavior: Explain the need for specialized treatment such as catheter intervention or surgical treatment including valve replacement and repair in valvular and congenital cardiac lesions.
Behavior: Obtain consent for physical examination and further investigations and treatment.

topics.title: Palpitations
objectives: Knowledge: The basic mechanism of palpitations.
Knowledge: List common causes of palpitations.
Knowledge: Define principles of managing the symptom discomfort.
Knowledge: Define specific management of the underlying disorder.
Skills: Differentiate physiological from pathological palpitations.

History: Elicit history of regularity/irregularity.
History: Elicit history of associated symptoms - dyspnoea/presyncope/chest pain.
Physical examination: Decipher pulse irregularity and apex/pulse deficit.
Physical examination: Elicit cardiac enlargement if present.
Physical examination: Differentiate the types of regurgitant lesions that cause palpitations.
Physical examination: Demonstrate corroborative signs such as left parasternal heave, peripheral signs of AR, late systolic heave of MR.
Differential diagnosis: Differentiate between VPCs and AF; differentiate between AR/MR/cardiomyopathy; understand common tachyarrhythmias - SVT/NSVT/AF.
Investigations: Propose a scheme of investigating palpitations in the following order: ECG; 24-hr Holter; loop recorder; echocardiography for structural disorders; chest XR for cardiomegaly.

topics.title: Hematuria
objectives: Knowledge: Differentiate microscopic and macroscopic (gross) hematuria.
Knowledge: Differentiate glomerular vs non-glomerular hematuria.
Knowledge: List the causes of glomerular and non-glomerular hematuria.
Skills: Demonstrate relevant history and examination skills pertaining to hematuria.
Skills: Differentiate local (genitourinary) from systemic disorders like vasculitis and autoimmune disease and intravascular hemolysis, G6PD, sickle cell disease.

Skills: Demonstrate correct method of collection of urine sample.

Skills: Differentiate blood in urine from RBC.

topics.title: Proteinuria
objectives: Knowledge: Define proteinuria and differentiate between transient and persistent proteinuria.

Knowledge: Suggest the indication of renal biopsy.

Skills: List specific investigations if indicated like autoimmune, vasculitis and other secondary glomerulonephritis workups.

Management: Determine when to obtain consultation from a nephrologist.

topics.title: Renal failure (Acute)

History taking: Determine history of fluid loss.

History taking: Medications (nephrotoxicity).

topics.title: Renal failure (Chronic)
objectives: Knowledge: Causes of chronic renal failure - pre-renal causes (renal vascular disease/occlusion, cholesterol/clot emboli); renal causes (glomerular diseases, primary: FSGS, IgA nephropathy; glomerular diseases, secondary: diabetic, hypertensive nephropathy, SLE; tubulo-interstitial: chronic interstitial nephritis from drug toxicity or infection, cystic kidney disease e.g. adult polycystic kidney disease/medullary kidney disease; vascular/ischemic nephropathy; congenital dysplasia); post-renal causes (obstructive nephropathy).

History: Identify patients at risk for chronic renal failure; ask about diabetes, hypertension, heart failure, past renal findings, and family history of kidney disease; diagnose chronic renal failure, its etiology, and complications (e.g., anemia); ask about symptoms during urination, recent infections, skin rash or arthritis, risk for parenterally transmitted disease (HIV, hepatitis).

Behavior: Emphasize falls prevention strategies with the nursing staff.
Behavior: Liaise with speech therapist for swallow assessment and advice for patients with motor neuron disease and bulbar palsy.

topics.title: Wheezing

Perform fundoscopy.
Diagnosis, investigations and management.

Causes of the pupillary abnormalities.
Diagnostic approach to causes of pupillary abnormalities.

topics.title: Approach to a child with painful limp/arthralgia
objectives: Goals: Elicit an appropriate history in a child presenting with arthralgia/painful limp; perform a detailed MSK system examination and relevant systemic examination; develop a differential diagnosis for a child presenting with limp/arthralgia; recognize common causes of limp in children (non-rheumatic); recognize some common rheumatologic diseases in children presenting with limp/arthralgia.

Knowledge: Recognize common causes of limp/arthralgia in children: trauma (stress fracture, traumatic epiphyseal injury); infections (septic arthritis, osteomyelitis); malignancy (leukemia, lymphoma, Ewing's sarcoma, osteoid osteoma); hematologic (sickle cell disease, hemophilia); inflammatory (reactive arthritis, toxic synovitis); rheumatic diseases (JIA, SLE, JDM, vasculitis); orthopedic conditions (hip: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, developmental dysplasia of the hip; knee: Osgood-Schlatter disease, chondromalacia patellae, patellar tendon partial rupture, osteochondritis, subluxation, dislocation, meniscal injuries, popliteal cyst); other non-inflammatory conditions such as growing pains of childhood.

History taking: Elicit a detailed history of the event including history of joint pain (number of joints, onset, duration, progression, relieving and aggravating factors, distribution, cumulative vs migratory joint pain, morning stiffness or gelling effect, ability to bear weight, degree of restriction in activity, impact on daily activity), preceding illness (fever, sore throat, dysentery, viral illness), trauma, recent antibiotics, immunization, travel history, drinking unpasteurized milk, TB contact; complete review of symptoms to exclude systemic illness; past medical illness; family history (autoimmune diseases, RA, SLE, IBD, uveitis, sickle cell disease); social history (impact of the illness on child and family, degree of parental anxiety).

Physical examination: Perform pGALS assessment as an initial screening tool; perform a detailed regional joint examination (look, feel, move); perform a detailed systemic examination to exclude systemic causes of limp.

Differential diagnosis: Based on history and physical examination, give a prioritized differential considering: trauma; infection (septic arthritis, osteomyelitis); inflammatory (reactive arthritis, toxic synovitis, acute rheumatic fever); rheumatic diseases (JIA, SLE, JDM, vasculitis - Kawasaki, HSP); hematology (hemophilia); malignancy (leukemia, lymphoma, Ewing's sarcoma); orthopedic conditions (AVN, SCFE, Osgood-Schlatter); other non-inflammatory (growing pain, hypermobility, fibromyalgia).

Laboratory interpretation: Give a prioritized list of laboratory investigations and interpretation when indicated including: CBC, inflammatory markers; blood culture; viral serology; joint aspiration and culture; bone marrow aspiration; radiological imaging (X-ray, ultrasound, bone scan, CT or MRI); rheumatological workup (ANA, dsDNA, ENA, RF, HLA B27).
Basic procedural skills: Observe joint aspiration if possible.
Communication skills: Discuss with peers and nurses concerning disease and treatment plan; counsel the parents about the cause of limping, treatment, and prognosis.

Management: Formulate an effective treatment plan for a child with limping based on underlying etiology; outline a plan of management of a child with JIA and appreciate differences of treatment in children versus adults; recognize the importance of a multidisciplinary approach in the management of children with rheumatic diseases.
Attitudes: Recognize the impact of the disease on the child and family; demonstrate empathy and sympathy to the child and family; offer support as needed.

Clinical tutorial learning objectives: Develop a systematic approach to a child presenting with joint pain; review MSK examination skills including pGALS and regional joint examination principles; differentiate between infectious, malignant, hematological, orthopedic, metabolic, and rheumatological causes of joint pain in children; understand the clinical presentation and general treatment principles for the differential diagnosis of joint pain in children.

topics.title: Approach to a child with an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis)
objectives: Goal: Define anaphylaxis, describe the characteristic signs and symptoms, identify causative agents, and formulate an emergency management plan.
Knowledge: Define anaphylaxis.

Knowledge: List several causes: foods (peanuts, nuts, seafood); drugs (beta-lactam antibiotics, NSAIDs, antineoplastic medications, ACEI); blood products; Hymenoptera (bees, wasps) envenomation; radiographic contrast media; latex.
Knowledge: Describe type-1 hypersensitivity immune-mediated reactions.
Knowledge: Discuss the pathophysiology of anaphylaxis and describe the typical course of events from exposure to an allergen to a life-threatening reaction.
Knowledge: Distinguish the difference between anaphylaxis and anaphylactoid reaction.
Knowledge: Describe biphasic reactions.
Knowledge: List the causes of mortality due to anaphylaxis.

History taking: Elicit a focused history about the histamine-mediated allergic reaction and list the symptoms and signs of anaphylaxis related to: skin; respiratory tract; gastrointestinal tract; cardiovascular system.

Physical examination: Perform ABC assessment on a patient with anaphylaxis; perform systematic assessment recognizing tachycardia, hypotension, shock, urticaria, angioedema, wheezing, upper airway obstruction.
Differential diagnosis: Differentiate clinically: anaphylaxis vs vasovagal syncope; systemic mastocytosis and hereditary angioedema; other causes of body swelling.
Laboratory interpretation: Recognize that diagnosis of anaphylaxis is mainly clinical (serum tryptase in the first 4 hours of the reaction may be helpful).
Basic procedural skills: Practice the administration of epinephrine (IM).

Communication skills: Communicate appropriately with the patient and family regarding the disease; describe the methods of prevention including carrying an injectable epinephrine; recognize the importance of educating school authorities about the patient's condition and precautionary measures (e.g. self-injectable epinephrine).

Management: Discuss the management of anaphylaxis: secure ABC; intramuscular administration of epinephrine; antihistamines; intravenous fluids; endotracheal intubation; corticosteroids; vasopressors. Discuss the relationship of idiopathic anaphylaxis and systemic mastocytosis. Identify that delayed administration of epinephrine is one of the leading causes of death.

Attitudes: Reflect responsibility and commitment towards patient management and wellbeing; recognize the impact of the disease on the patient's life & family; identify the anxiety of the patient and family about anaphylaxis secondary to accidental exposures to an allergen.

topics.title: Approach to a child with breathing difficulty
objectives: Goals: Define breathing difficulty in children; differentiate between upper airway and lower airway causes of breathing difficulty; understand the classification of severity of shortness of breath by clinical symptoms; formulate a management plan for a child with breathing difficulty.
Knowledge: Definition of respiratory distress.
Knowledge: Classification of respiratory failure (type 1 - hypoxic & type II - hypercapnic).

Knowledge: Causes of respiratory distress - airway problems (croup, foreign body aspiration, laryngeal edema/spasm/epiglottitis, retropharyngeal abscess); pulmonary problems (tracheitis/bronchiolitis, pneumonia, asthma/bronchospasm); cardiac problems (congestive heart failure, acyanotic congenital heart disease such as VSD, ASD, cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolus); pleural problems (pleural effusion, empyema, pneumothorax).
Knowledge: Differentiation between upper and lower airway obstruction based on anatomical location, presentation, causes, and management.
Knowledge: Discuss the pathophysiology, clinical presentation, radiological findings and specific management for each cause of respiratory distress.
Knowledge: Assessment of severity of breathing difficulty.
Knowledge: Management of chronic cough and acute exacerbations of chronic cough conditions.

History taking: Age and time of onset (acute vs chronic); progress of symptoms; associated symptoms (fever, cough - barking or paroxysmal, drooling of saliva, difficulty in swallowing, URTI, diurnal variation, triggering and relieving factors); prior use of nebulization; cyanosis, increased work of breathing, lethargy; associated vomiting (post-tussive emesis), hemoptysis; exposure (bukhoor, smoking, wood-burning, dust, pollution, animals, allergens); history of choking/suspected aspiration of a foreign body; prenatal and neonatal history; immunization history; developmental history; family history of atopic disease (asthma, allergic rhinitis, eczema).

Physical examination: ABC (airway, breathing, circulation); vital signs (heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation); growth parameters; look for clubbing, cachexia, edema, cyanosis, general stigmata of chronic disease; signs of respiratory distress (suprasternal, subcostal/intercostal retractions); inspect the chest wall for deformities and signs of hyperinflation; palpate for tracheal deviation; auscultate thoroughly for air entry and added sounds; auscultate heart sounds and murmurs; look for hepatomegaly; systemic examination.

Differential diagnosis: Based on clinical findings - respiratory distress with wheezy chest indicates lower airway obstruction (asthma, bronchiolitis, foreign body aspiration); respiratory distress with stridor indicates upper airway obstruction (toxic appearance: epiglottitis, tracheitis, retropharyngeal abscess; nontoxic appearance: croup); respiratory distress with crepitations (bronchopneumonia, heart failure); respiratory distress with normal chest examination (CNS insult, postictal).

Laboratory interpretation: Complete blood count (look for high WBC, neutrophilia, or lymphocytosis); CRP; nasopharyngeal aspirate for respiratory viral screen; sputum cultures; blood culture; chest X-ray and neck XR (indications, signs of pleural effusion, signs of pulmonary edema, measuring cardiac shadow for cardiomegaly, lateral/AP neck signs - steeple sign, thumb sign, retropharyngeal abscess, shaggy trachea for tracheitis); CT chest.
Basic procedural skills: Bag-mask ventilation using head tilt chin lift or jaw thrust; choose the appropriate size of the mask and oral airway.
Communication skills: Elicit a detailed history from the family to identify potential causes; counsel the family about investigations, potential treatments, and prognosis.

Management: Use the Pediatric Assessment Triangle to identify critically sick children; stabilization and management of children with respiratory distress per PALS guidelines - primary survey (airway: patent or not, suction if required; breathing: saturation, RR, auscultation findings, 100% oxygen via non-rebreathing mask, nebulization according to clinical finding; circulation: CRT, HR, BP, pulse volume, secure IV access, 10-20 ml/kg fluid bolus if required; disability and dextrose: check blood sugar, pupils, GCS or AVPU; exposure: body temperature and skin rash); secondary survey (head-to-toe examination, SAMPLE history); tertiary survey (investigation, imaging).
Attitudes: Identify life-threatening respiratory failure; be able to initiate stabilization measures for a child with respiratory distress.

topics.title: Approach to a child with fever and rash
objectives: Goals: Identify the important points in history and perform a detailed physical examination in a child presenting with fever and rash; describe the most common primary skin lesions in a child with fever and rash; explain the most common differential diagnosis of fever and rash; be aware of the infection control measures of the common infections presenting with fever and rash; identify that children with fever and maculopapular rash should be notified to the Ministry of Health as a suspected case of 'Fever and Rash illness' syndrome; explain the diagnosis and management of Kawasaki disease.

History taking: Patient age; detailed history of fever including exposures (mosquito, animals, ticks, etc.) and travel history; details of the onset, characteristics, distribution, and progression of the rash, the timing of onset in relation to the fever, associated systemic manifestations, and prior contact with persons having a similar illness; medical background including immune status; family history of skin diseases, allergy, atopy, and rheumatological problems; medication history; immunization history.

Physical examination: Describe the general look and how sick the child is; perform good general, dermatological, and other systemic examinations; check vital signs for fever, tachycardia, and hypotension (shock); detailed examination of lymph nodes; abdominal examination for organomegaly; examination of the entire body surface, mucus membrane, conjunctiva, hair, and nails with adequate illumination - describe and differentiate primary skin lesions and extent of skin involvement; examine oral cavity for Koplik's spots, red cracked lips, strawberry tongue, red enlarged tonsils with whitish membrane; eye examination for conjunctivitis (purulent/non-purulent); changes in the extremities including erythema, swelling, and peeling of palms and soles.

Differential diagnosis: Based on history and physical examination, list differential diagnoses starting with common infections: viral (infectious mononucleosis, adenovirus infection, hand foot and mouth disease, herpes simplex virus, chickenpox, measles, erythema infectiosum, roseola infantum); bacterial (meningococcemia, scarlet fever, staphylococcal skin infection, impetigo, acute rheumatic fever, toxic shock syndrome); vasculitis like Kawasaki disease; rheumatological problems like juvenile idiopathic arthritis; malignancy; drug reaction; others like erythema multiforme and Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

Laboratory investigations: Understand that not all patients require investigations - blood culture and FBC in patients who look sick and if the child has purpura or petechiae; skin swab for gram stain, microscopy, and culture if bacterial infection suspected; Tzanck smear/PCR for HSV and VZV; measles serology and PCR from throat and urine if measles suspected; CMV and EBV serology in infectious mononucleosis; echocardiogram if Kawasaki disease suspected; skin biopsy in consultation with dermatology in the minority of cases.
Basic procedural skills: Collect skin swab.

Communication skills: Briefly discuss the management plans of the common infections presenting with fever and rash; counsel the families about management, expected course, prognosis, and the importance of infection control strategies if required.

Management: Explain the management of: chickenpox; measles; infectious mononucleosis; hand foot and mouth disease; scarlet fever; meningococcemia; toxic shock syndrome; Kawasaki disease. Understand the importance of hand hygiene and infection control requirements. Mandatory notification for patients with fever and maculopapular rash as suspected 'Fever and Rash illness' syndrome.

Attitudes: Demonstrate the importance of isolating any child with fever and rash until clinical assessment; demonstrate urgency in managing children who present with fever and skin rash as in meningococcal infection and toxic shock syndrome; allay anxiety of parents; realize the importance of constantly communicating with parents about progress in the treatment of sick children.

Clinical tutorial learning objectives (Kawasaki disease): Know the diagnostic criteria for KD; list differential diagnoses including infectious and allergic conditions that resemble KD; name the appropriate management of Kawasaki disease.

Clinical tutorial learning objectives (measles): Understand the common signs and symptoms of measles; list differential diagnoses; understand the importance of travel and immunization history; name appropriate investigations and management; infection control and mandatory notification to MOH.

Clinical tutorial learning objectives (meningococcal sepsis): Understand the urgency of managing sick patients with fever and rash; know the common presentation of meningococcal sepsis; list differential diagnoses; name the appropriate management; mandatory notification to MOH and chemoprophylaxis to household contacts.

topics.title: Approach to fever in children less than a year of age
objectives: Goals: Recognize the different clinical approaches (in terms of investigations and treatment) to a febrile child based on age: less than 28 days of age (neonate), 1-3 months, and 3-36 months; recall the indications and contraindications for doing a lumbar puncture; recall the different methods used to collect urine sample for culture and sensitivity based on the child's age and how to interpret the results.
Knowledge: Definition of fever in children.
