Knowledge: Specific findings on history and examination that could guide towards a focus of infection in a febrile child.
Knowledge: The most common pathogens causing infections in the first year of life.
Knowledge: Reasons why young infants are at increased risk of infection and meningitis from certain pathogens.
Knowledge: Risk factors for UTI in young infants.
Knowledge: Approach to investigation and treatment of a child with fever based on age: less than 28 days (neonate), 1-3 months, and 3-36 months.
Knowledge: The different predictors including signs and symptoms suggestive of CNS infection across different age groups.
Knowledge: Indications and contraindications of lumbar puncture, and the steps needed to perform the procedure.
Knowledge: Urine collection methods for urinalysis and urine culture, and their interpretations.

History taking: Age at onset; severity of fever, duration, pattern, association with sweats or chills; fever with headaches, lethargy, altered consciousness, seizures, or weakness (CNS infection); fever with respiratory symptoms (pneumonia); fever with fatigue, swollen lymph nodes, or sore throat (EBV); fever with abdominal discomfort, vomiting, or diarrhea (gastroenteritis); fever with musculoskeletal complaints (septic arthritis or osteomyelitis); fever with a rash (meningococcemia); antenatal infections, cold sores, and GBS swab results (early-onset neonatal sepsis, HSV infections); fever with travel (tuberculosis, malaria, typhoid); history of animal exposure (cat scratch disease, brucellosis, Q fever, salmonella); food exposure, unpasteurized dairy, undercooked meat (brucellosis, Q fever, salmonella, toxoplasmosis); family history of recent infection; medication exposure (drug fever).

Physical examination: Correct measurement of core body temperature; vital signs including height and weight (growth chart); general examination including hydration status and mental status; HEENT (conjunctivae, tympanic membranes, sinuses, mouth and throat, lymph nodes); chest (tachypnea, abnormal breath sounds); heart (tachycardia, murmurs, stigmata of endocarditis); GI tract (hepatosplenomegaly, tenderness); skin (rash, bruises, petechiae); skeletal (bone or joint abnormalities); lymphadenopathy; neurologic (mental status, CNs, opsoclonus-myoclonus, meningeal signs, gait); hospitalized patients: medical devices.

Investigations: Review previous results; CBC with peripheral smear; U&E, bone profile; LFTs; ESR and CRP; urinalysis and urine culture; blood culture; chest x-ray; CSF microscopy, glucose, protein, and microbiology (bacterial culture and viral PCRs); targeted investigations based on findings on history and examination.
Basic procedural skills: Measuring temperature.

Communication skills: Elicit a detailed history from the family to identify potential causes; counsel the family about the possible diagnosis, the needed basic investigations, lumbar puncture (indications, possible complications, procedure's steps, and risk of not obtaining CSF sample in a timely manner), urine culture collection methods; be able to gain the confidence of the family despite not having a clear diagnosis initially.

Management: Thorough history and physical examination and required basic investigations; how to interpret CSF results and the likely infectious organisms; IV antibiotics need to be started for suspected cases based on age group; empirical antibiotic choices based on child age, clinical severity, and likely fever-causative organisms.

Attitudes: Understand the need for urgent management for a child with fever in the neonatal period (0-28 days of life); work professionally in a multidisciplinary team including nursing, laboratories, radiologists, critical care units; maintain good infection control practices when an infection is suspected.

topics.title: Approach to a child with pallor
objectives: Goals: Recognize common hematological conditions in children presenting with anemia; know how to manage common anemias in pediatrics; counsel the families effectively.

Knowledge: Understand the etiological classification of anemia - poor production (nutrient deficiency: iron deficiency anemia, B12 & folic acid deficiency; bone marrow failure: pure red cell aplasia, Fanconi anemia, acquired aplastic anemia; bone marrow infiltration: leukemia, lymphoma, neuroblastoma, lipid storage disorders); increased destruction/hemolysis (hemoglobinopathies: sickle cell disease & thalassemia; enzymopathies: G6PD deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency; membranopathies: hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis; microangiopathic hemolytic anemia: DIC, TTP, HUS; autoimmune hemolytic anemia; sequestrations such as acute splenic sequestration in SCD); increased loss/hemorrhagic anemia (acute blood loss: road traffic accidents, trauma; chronic blood loss: diaphragmatic hernia, hemorrhoids).

History taking: Take a detailed history of the pallor including how it was discovered, onset, course, duration, any treatment given, associated manifestations (bone aches, swelling of hands/feet, fever, shortness of breath, abdominal distension), color of urine and stool, jaundice, easy fatigability, blood loss from body orifices, and triggering factors such as certain foods or medications; history of simple blood transfusion and/or exchange transfusion; past history including neonatal screening for G6PD and hemoglobinopathies, prolonged or recurrent hospital admission; family history of consanguinity and hematological disorders; drug history (iron or multivitamin therapy, hydroxyurea, folic acid, analgesics, chemotherapy); full nutritional history including age of weaning, number of meals, and type of food.

Physical examination: Skin and mucous membranes - assess for pallor in the palms, lips, tongue, and conjunctiva; examine skin and conjunctiva for jaundice in natural light; check for mucocutaneous bleeding tendency, cafe au lait spots; examination of hands/feet especially in infants with suspected SCD. General examination - assessment of general condition, signs of infections, congenital anomalies, dysmorphic features; detailed examination of lymph nodes; cardiac examination (gallop or hemic murmurs); chest examination (mediastinal masses, consolidation); abdominal examination for organomegaly.
Differential diagnosis: Based on history and physical examination, formulate a list of differential diagnoses and generate a plan of investigations.

Laboratory interpretation: Know the normal age-adjusted values of complete blood count and how to interpret abnormal findings; understand the significance of red cell indices, reticulocyte count and RDW; classify anemia as hypochromic/microcytic, normochromic/normocytic, or macrocytic based on lab results; recognize common blood film abnormalities (RBC morphology, abnormal cells); interpret age-adjusted hemoglobin electrophoresis results and differentiate normal from abnormal neonatal screening results; understand the significance of hemolytic markers (hemoglobinuria, reticulocyte count, bilirubin, haptoglobin, LDH); know the lab profile of common nutritional anemias (Fe deficiency, B12, folate deficiency); understand the concept of iron overload and its follow-up in thalassemia; recognize the utility of imaging (US and MRI) in assessment and follow-up of sickle cell disease patients.
Basic procedural skills: Observe bone marrow aspiration; bone marrow trephine biopsy; exchange transfusion for patients with sickle cell disease.

Communication skills: Discuss management plans of various causes of anemia in children; counsel families about management, expected course, and prognosis; understand the concept of hydroxyurea therapy and explain it to families; provide sound genetic counseling; teach parents how to examine the spleen in cases of SCD to predict the risk of acute splenic sequestration.

Management: Formulate an effective short- and long-term management plan of SCD in pediatrics; understand a simple management plan for patients with SCD presenting with different types of crises; know how to manage Fe deficiency anemia, calculate the dose of oral Fe therapy, and provide proper dietary recommendations; recognize the concept of hydroxyurea therapy for SCD; understand the role of iron chelating agents for patients with thalassemia; figure out the role of BMT as a curative therapy for chronic hemolytic anemias.
Attitudes: Recognize the impact of the disease on the child and family; demonstrate empathy and sympathy to the child and family; offer support as needed.

topics.title: Approach to a child with a bleeding tendency
objectives: Goals: Obtain a proper history in a child presenting with bleeding tendency/easy bruising; differentiate between non-accidental injury and disorders of hemostasis; perform a detailed clinical examination including general examination, assessment of mucocutaneous bleeding, abdominal examination, and MSK examination; get clues from history and examination to differentiate between coagulation and bleeding disorders; know when to refer pediatric cases with a significant bleeding tendency; plan a stepwise approach of investigations tailored for each case; interpret the results of hematological investigations accurately; recognize common hematological conditions in children presenting with bleeding tendency; manage acute bleeding episodes in some common pediatric disorders; counsel the families effectively.

Knowledge: Bleeding disorders - decrease in number (decreased production: bone marrow failure/BM infiltration - leukemia, lymphoma; increased destruction: immune-mediated - ITP, Evans syndrome; non-immune-mediated - microangiopathy: DIC, HUS, TTP; abnormal sequestration: acute splenic sequestration, Kasabach-Merritt syndrome); platelet dysfunction (congenital: VWD, Bernard-Soulier syndrome, Glanzmann's; acquired: drugs such as aspirin, NSAIDs); vascular disorders (Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, scurvy); coagulation disorders (hemophilia, VWD, factor deficiencies, hypofibrinogenemia); non-accidental injury.

History taking: Take a detailed history of the bleeding episode including onset, course, duration, aggravating and relieving factors, recurrence, sites, mucosal involvement, and bleeding from orifices (epistaxis, gingival bleeding, hematemesis, hemoptysis, hematuria, melena, hematochezia); history of preceding URTI and associated manifestations; history of surgical challenges, post-procedural bleeding, post-circumcision bleeding, bleeding after dental extraction, bleeding from umbilical stump, or post-vaccination; nature of bleeding (superficial or deep-sited, acute or recurrent, mucocutaneous or musculoskeletal); rule out non-accidental injury (child abuse) in cases of multiple types of injuries, variable ages of bruises, suspicious family dynamics, unclear mechanism of injury; family history of bleeding tendency (especially maternal uncles/grandfather for hemophilia), surgical challenges, menorrhagia (VWD or platelet function disorders), consanguinity; drug history (aspirin, NSAIDs, heparin, oral anticoagulants, chemotherapeutic agents); social history to rule out child abuse; vaccination history; menstrual history in teens.

Physical examination: Skin and mucous membranes - differentiate between purpura, petechiae, ecchymosis, and contusions; perform slide test to confirm purpuric spots do not blanch with pressure; examine oral cavity, gingiva, and conjunctivae for mucosal bleeding; recognize skin lesions similar to purpuric spots (meningococcemia rash, purpura fulminans, palpable purpura of HSP). General examination - general condition, signs of infections, pallor, congenital anomalies, dysmorphic features; detailed lymph node examination; abdominal examination for organomegaly; full MSK examination; CNS examination for focal neurological deficits and signs of lateralization.

Differential diagnosis: Based on history and physical examination, list differential diagnoses - bleeding disorders (ITP, acute leukemia, aplastic anemia, medications, platelet dysfunction); coagulation disorders (hemophilia, VWD, other factor deficiencies, hypofibrinogenemia, factor XIII deficiency).

Laboratory interpretation: Know the normal values of complete blood count and interpret abnormal findings; recognize common blood film abnormalities; know normal values of coagulation screen (PT, aPTT, TT) and identify causes of prolongation in relation to the coagulation cascade; understand the basics of mixing study to differentiate factor deficiency from circulating inhibitors; establish a scheme of stepwise investigations based on clinical status and lab abnormalities; stress that bleeding history is a key milestone in diagnosis; know the indications of bone marrow aspiration (leukemia, bone marrow failure, atypical ITP with cytopenias or organomegaly); recognize that rare disorders (factor XIII deficiency, platelet function disorders) need further workup; understand the role of bedside US and MRI to assess hemarthrosis and target joints in hemophilia.
Basic procedural skills: Observe bone marrow aspiration; bone marrow trephine biopsy; bedside US for hemarthrosis.

Communication skills: Discuss management plans of various bleeding disorders; counsel families about management, expected course, and prognosis; explain an observation plan for ITP, estimate bleeding risk based on family dynamics, convey recommendations regarding avoidance of contact sports, NSAIDs, and IM injections; understand the concept of prophylactic home therapy and explain it to families of hemophiliacs; provide sound genetic counseling to patients affected with hemophilia.

Management: Formulate an effective management plan of acute and chronic ITP in pediatrics; understand a simple management plan for patients with hemophilia presenting with acute bleeding episodes; recognize the concepts of prophylactic treatment and home therapy for hemophilia; understand the role of factor replacement therapy for VWD and other factor deficiencies; figure out the role of bypassing agents in the management of hemophilia with inhibitors.
Attitudes: Recognize the impact of the disease on the child and family; demonstrate empathy and sympathy to the child and family; offer support as needed.

topics.title: Approach to common neonatal problems
objectives: Goals: Recognize the clinical presentation of common neonatal problems; develop a management plan for common neonatal problems; counsel a mother of a newborn baby with neonatal problems on outcome and prognosis; understand how to evaluate and manage common conditions in newborns (thermoregulation: risk factors, clinical presentation, pathophysiology, and management of hypothermia; common causes of respiratory distress in a newborn: transient tachypnea of newborns, pneumonia, respiratory distress in preterm newborns, meconium aspiration syndrome; neonatal sepsis: differentiate early and late-onset sepsis, clinical signs and symptoms, investigations and management; hypoglycemia; neonatal jaundice: differentiate causes of indirect hyperbilirubinemia including pathological, physiological and breast milk jaundice, risk factors, pathophysiology, investigations and management; birth asphyxia: clinical manifestations and AAP diagnostic criteria of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE); common skin rashes/conditions: erythema toxicum, Mongolian spot, milia, neonatal acne, neonatal pustular melanosis, hemangioma).
Knowledge: Define the following: perinatal period; neonatal period; normal birth weight; low birth weight (LBW); very low birth weight (VLBW); extremely LBW (ELBW).
Knowledge: Recognize the normal values in newborns: heart rate; respiratory rate; normal temperature; normal oxygen saturation; APGAR score.

History taking: Booked case or un-booked case; outcome of previous gestations; obtain history of maternal drug intake, hypertension, and diabetes in pregnancy; maternal serology to rule out infectious diseases (HIV, Hep B, syphilis); identify maternal risk factors for neonatal sepsis (prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis); blood group - recognize the importance of ABO and Rh incompatibility as a cause of hemolytic jaundice on day one of life; history of present illness related to feeding problems, vomiting, diarrhea, lethargy, irritability, difficulty in breathing, excessive crying, pallor.

Physical examination: General (pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, acrocyanosis); vital signs (hypothermia, hyperthermia, tachycardia, bradycardia, hypotension, oxygen saturation); head and neck examination; heart (murmur, weak pulses, large liver, central vs acrocyanosis); respiratory (signs of distress: flaring, grunting, tachypnea, intercostal and subcostal recession); neurologic (tone, power and reflexes).

Laboratory interpretation: CBC - recognize leukocytosis, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia in neonatal sepsis; anemia and increased reticulocyte count in acute hemolysis; biochemical abnormalities (sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium - hypernatremia with dehydration; SIADH in RDS or fluid overload; glucose monitoring in sick term babies, preterm babies, infants of diabetic mothers, low birth weight infants); blood gas - identify and differentiate causes of respiratory and metabolic acidosis; blood culture, CSF analysis and urine culture in all newborns with suspected sepsis; blood group and Coombs test for ABO incompatibility and immune hemolytic anemia; chest x-rays (endotracheal tube placement, heart size and vascularity, differentiate transient tachypnea, pneumonia, RDS, meconium aspiration); abdominal x-rays to locate umbilical venous lines.

Basic procedural skills: Observe procedures during care of preterm neonates: IV cannulation; umbilical arterial and venous lines; blood collection (heel pricking, central/umbilical line); routine care in NICU.

Communication skills: Discuss with colleagues and nurses regarding the treatment plan for the newborn; counsel and educate parents about the reason for the disease, possible course of illness, required therapy, expected complications and chances for survival; describe unit protocols for prevention of sepsis.

Management: Management of respiratory distress in term newborn (oxygen, IV fluids, minimal handling; may deteriorate requiring CPAP or mechanical ventilation); management of neonatal sepsis and pneumonia with appropriate antibiotics; management of neonatal jaundice (indirect hyperbilirubinemia) with phototherapy, exchange transfusion and good hydration; management of birth asphyxia.

Attitudes: Recognize the importance of handwashing and hygiene strictly followed in the neonatal unit; recognize and appreciate the disruption to the family with an ill baby in the hospital; reflect responsibility and commitment towards the patient's management and wellbeing; recognize that during the illness of the newborn the whole family is under extreme mental and physical stress and needs full concern and support.

topics.title: Approach to a child with failure to thrive
objectives: Knowledge: Define failure to thrive.
Knowledge: Differentiate between organic and non-organic causes of FTT.
Knowledge: Recognize that organic causes of FTT are classified according to prenatal, perinatal, and postnatal causes.
Knowledge: Identify some prenatal causes of FTT such as prematurity, placental insufficiency, antenatal infection, placental or chromosomal abnormalities, exposure to toxins, maternal factors.
Knowledge: Identify some perinatal causes of FTT which include: acutely ill neonate - hypoxic ischemia.

Knowledge: Identify and classify some postnatal causes of FTT: increased metabolic demand (hyperthyroidism, chronic diseases such as CHF, chronic inflammatory conditions, renal failure, malignancy); poor absorption (celiac disease, cystic fibrosis, malabsorptive enteropathy, inflammatory bowel disease); poor oral intake (inability to suck and swallow due to CNS disease, GERD).
Knowledge: Discuss some non-organic causes of FTT such as child neglect, difficult parent-child bonding, dysfunctional family, and other environmental factors.
Knowledge: Recognize that FTT can result from a combination of both organic and non-organic causes.
Knowledge: Differentiate FTT from other causes of growth delay such as constitutional growth delay, endocrine causes such as growth hormone deficiency, as well as other chromosomal/genetic causes.
History taking: Obtain, document and present detailed history including an assessment of diet, feeding, eating behaviors; past and current medical, social, and family history relevant to FTT.

Physical examination: Identify dysmorphic features suggestive of a genetic disorder affecting growth; detect an underlying disease that may impair growth; assess for signs of possible child abuse; assess the severity and possible effects of malnutrition.
Differential diagnosis: Generate a prioritized differential diagnosis.

Laboratory interpretation: Propose and interpret diagnostic and laboratory tests for a child with failure to thrive - laboratory and diagnostic tests when appropriate may include: CBC, U&E, LFT, urinalysis and culture, stool studies for parasites; more specific tests when clinically indicated include: HIV, sweat chloride, thyroid function test, immunoglobulins, stool studies for malabsorption and endomysial antibody screen for celiac disease.
Communication skills: Communicate the diagnosis and specific treatment plan for the individual situation with the family.

Management: Design an appropriate evaluation and treatment plan for patients; recognize the indications for hospitalization to treat FTT; provide adequate dietary advice with the addition of supplements when required; counsel about appropriate feeding behaviors.

Attitudes: Listen attentively to elicit and synthesize the relevant information of the patient's illness; recognize the psychosocial effect of the illness on the child and his family; communicate effectively with colleagues, faculty, and patients; interact with other professionals involved in patient care through effective teamwork.

topics.title: Approach to immunization in children
objectives: Goals: Know different vaccines used in the immunization schedule in Oman; describe the morbidity and mortality associated with different diseases that are prevented by these vaccines; appreciate the value of immunization through reduction of diseases and children's mortality rate.
Knowledge: Know the basic immune response to a vaccine.
Knowledge: Understand the types of immunity (active and passive) with examples.
Knowledge: Know the types of vaccines and routes of administration.

Knowledge: Know individual vaccines (BCG, Hepatitis B vaccine HBV, oral and inactivated polio vaccines OPV/IPV, Diphtheria-Pertussis-Tetanus vaccine DPT, Hemophilus influenzae b vaccine HiB, Pneumococcal vaccine PCV, Measles-Mumps-Rubella vaccine MMR, Varicella vaccine, and Hepatitis A vaccine).
Knowledge: Recognize the dosing schedule for each vaccine as listed in the immunization card.
Knowledge: Describe the complications associated with individual diseases prevented by these vaccines with particular reference to morbidity and mortality.
Knowledge: Realize the effectiveness of individual vaccines in reducing/eliminating the disease.
Knowledge: Know the side effects following immunization - common such as fever, pain and swelling; very rare such as anaphylaxis and Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Knowledge: List the contraindications to vaccines such as live attenuated vaccines in the immunodeficient.
Knowledge: List other vaccines that are not part of the schedule such as seasonal influenza vaccine, meningococcal vaccine, rotavirus vaccine, rabies vaccine.
Knowledge: Recognize hyper immunoglobulin use in post-exposure prophylaxis such as hepatitis B hyper immunoglobulin.

History taking: Elicit the age of receiving the vaccines at different age schedule (birth, 2, 4, 6, 12, 13, 18 and 24 months); find if the child missed a certain vaccine and the reason; recognize any side effects experienced after any vaccine dose; ask if the child developed a scar after BCG vaccine; recognize that prior to BCG the parents are asked about family history of immunodeficiency; recognize that prior to each vaccine dose the parents are asked about reaction to the previous dose; elicit history of febrile convulsion/seizure disorder; elicit if there is a history of bleeding disorder.

Physical examination: Prior to each vaccination perform: vital signs including temperature; general examination; growth measures (weight, height, head circumference); systemic examination; examine for presence of BCG scar; examine for BCG adenitis (left axillary lymphadenitis). If the child has moderate/severe illness at due vaccination time, the vaccination should be postponed. Examine the immunization/health card and note documented previous vaccine doses. Document growth measures on the graphs in the health card every visit.
Assessment: Assess whether the child can be vaccinated during this visit; assess any other medical issues such as deviation from normal growth curves or developmental delay.
Laboratory interpretation: Children visiting for immunization are healthy and well at the time of immunization and don't require investigations.
Communication skills: Elicit a detailed history from the family; counsel the family about potential side effects such as fever and swelling at the injection site.

Management: Observe vaccine preparation and administration by the immunization nurse; after immunization prescribe antipyretic to be taken in case of fever; address any other medical issues encountered during this visit.

Attitudes: Work professionally in a multidisciplinary team including nursing, technicians and healthcare workers; maintain good infection control practices when handling, preparing and administering the vaccine.

topics.title: Child safety and prevention of accidental and non-accidental injuries
objectives: Goals: Enable the qualified physician to identify, treat and prevent various types of accidental and non-accidental injuries in children to ensure child safety.

Knowledge (accidental injuries/trauma): Know the relation of developmental characteristics to accidental injuries; know about the safety of toys and prevention of choking in children; have adequate knowledge about the management and prevention of road traffic accidents, falls, drowning, burns, scalds, poisoning, reptile and animal-related injuries; know the management and prevention of common poisons; know the consequences of trauma and the measures to prevent it.

Knowledge (non-accidental injuries/child abuse): Know the definition of child abuse/non-accidental injury; know the classification of child abuse (physical abuse, emotional abuse, child maltreatment/neglect - nutritional neglect, medical neglect/LAMA, sexual abuse, emotional or psychological abuse, Munchausen's syndrome by proxy); know the risk factors of child abuse (related to parents or caregivers, child, family, society/community/school); know the clinical characteristics of non-accidental injury and be aware of abnormal child behavior as a warning sign of child abuse.

History taking: Take a comprehensive history about the injury (type, time, date, place, witness, seriousness, detailed description of each injury); description of each injury, events following injury, details of medical care received, and colored photographs of the injury; check whether the given description can explain the type of injury; take detailed history about pregnancy, birth, growth, development, immunization, nutrition, systemic inquiry, past history, family history, social history, and medications; take history of risk factors of child abuse and ask about any abnormal behavior of the child.

Physical examination: Perform a complete physical examination including general examination, vital signs, congenital anomalies, dysmorphic features, mental state, and signs of infections; examine the skin especially back and buttocks for bruises, burns, scalds, bite marks, metal marks, finger and hand marks; perform a structured head-to-foot examination and systemic examination; examine the CNS for focal neurological deficit, abdomen for internal hemorrhage, chest for fractured ribs, musculoskeletal system for fractures, and eyes for retinal and conjunctival hemorrhage; examine the mucous membranes of the mouth, genitalia, ear, nose, and throat for injuries.

Differential diagnosis: Based on history and physical examination, make a reasonable medical judgment and a list of differential diagnoses: sepsis (CNS infection, meningococcemia); non-accidental injury; accidental injuries such as head injury; hematological diseases; bone disease causing pathological fracture; diseases like neuroblastoma in infants presenting as raccoon eyes.

Laboratory interpretation: Order investigations based on history and clinical examination in a prioritized manner and interpret results correctly - know normal and abnormal CBC values and interpretation of abnormal blood film findings in sepsis and malignancy; know normal values of coagulation screen (PT, APTT, TT) and causes of prolongation; know the importance of septic workup; identify abnormalities in skeletal survey (accidental and non-accidental injuries, pathological fractures); know the role of ultrasound or CT abdomen in abdominal trauma; know the importance of checking for bacteria and sperms in vaginal swabs in sexual abuse along with HIV and Hepatitis B; do a pregnancy test in adolescent girls in cases of sexual abuse.
Basic procedural skills: Observe fundoscopy; IV cannulation; CT scan of brain, MRI brain, and US/CT abdomen.

Communication skills: Discuss with caregivers about the management plan and the role of adequate supervision in the prevention of injuries; educate the family and community about prevention of accidental injuries (road traffic injuries, falls, choking, drowning, electric shock, burns, poisoning, animal and reptile related injuries); educate on the importance of communication and coordination with other subspecialties, child protection team, social worker, legal authorities in the management of non-accidental injuries.

Management: Recognize injuries and manage immediately with the guidance of an expert in an appropriate center; coordinate care involving a multidisciplinary team including pediatrician, subspecialist, child protection team, social worker, police, and public prosecution; recognize the importance of entering the child's name in a register of 'at-risk children' if indicated; identify the importance of separating the child from caregivers when there is a risk of recurrence; be aware of consequences and fatalities and manage complications with the help of experts; recognize the importance of primary and secondary prevention of child abuse and the role of community health education.
Attitudes: Recognize the impact of accidental and non-accidental injuries on the child, family, society, community; demonstrate empathy and sympathy to the child and family; offer support as needed.

topics.title: Approach to an infant with BRUE/SIDS
objectives: Goals: Define brief resolved unexplained event (BRUE); describe the symptoms of BRUE; evaluate an infant with BRUE; discuss appropriate investigations and management of an infant with BRUE; differentiate between BRUE and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS); delineate risk factors and prevention recommendations for SIDS; explain the updated American Academy of Pediatrics recommendations for a safe infant sleeping environment.

Knowledge: Define and describe: clinical features of BRUE and how it differs from SIDS; frightening episodes mimicking BRUE; assessment and management of an infant with BRUE; recommendations for a safe infant sleeping environment and to prevent SIDS.

History taking: History of the event (general description, who reported the event, witness, reliability of historian); state immediately before the event (where it occurred, awake or asleep, position, feeding, choking hazards); state during the event (choking or gagging noise, active or flaccid, consciousness, muscle tone, repetitive movements, distress, breathing, skin and lip color, bleeding); end of event (duration, how it stopped, abrupt or gradual); state after the event; recent history (illness in preceding days, injuries, falls, previous unexplained bruising); past medical history (pre-/perinatal history, gestational age, newborn screen, previous episodes/BRUE, reflux, breathing problems, snoring, growth, development, hospitalizations, immunization, OTC medications); family history (sudden unexplained death, BRUE in sibling, long QT syndrome, arrhythmia, IEM or genetic disease, developmental delay); social history (housing, family structure, exposure to smoke/toxic substances/drugs, recent infections, family anxiety, child protective services involvement, exposure to adults with mental illness or substance abuse); considerations for possible child abuse (multiple or changing versions of the history, history inconsistent with child's developmental stage, history of unexplained bruising).

Physical examination: Full physical examination from head to toe including general appearance, growth parameters, vital signs, skin (bruising or erythema), eyes (conjunctival hemorrhage), nose and mouth (coryza, torn frenulum), chest, heart, abdomen, genitalia, extremities (fracture) and full neurological assessment.

Differential diagnosis: Conditions that can present with a brief apneic event but are not BRUE: upper and lower respiratory infections (bronchiolitis, pertussis, pneumonia), sepsis, meningitis, gastroesophageal reflux, seizures, breath-holding spells, prolonged QT syndrome, arrhythmia, metabolic disorders or hypoglycemia, drug intoxication, and child abuse & neglect.

Laboratory interpretation: Understand that in lower-risk BRUE current guidelines recommend minimal testing, however nasopharyngeal swab for pertussis and ECG may be done in ER; recognize that in higher-risk infants initial tests include CBC, electrolytes, CRP, glucose, cultures, blood gas, chest X-ray, ECG plus further investigations based on clinical presentation and referral to relevant specialties; recognize the role of an autopsy to exclude different causes of SIDS in addition to toxic & metabolic screen and skeletal survey.

Communication skills: Take a detailed history of the event (before, during, and after); estimate the risk of BRUE (low or high risk) based on history, physical exam findings, event, and patient characteristics, and counsel the families about management; counsel the frightened parents of BRUE and the grieving parents of SIDS; counsel parents about prevention of SIDS and safe infant sleeping environment.

Management: Educate caregivers about the condition, ensure close follow-up after discharge, and provide resources for training in cardiopulmonary resuscitation; in low-risk BRUE admission for monitoring is not routinely indicated - no role for medications, tests, specialist consultations; high-risk infants need admission and should be managed based on abnormalities identified in history and physical exam; recognize the role of autopsy in SIDS diagnosis (other investigations: toxic screen, metabolic screen, skeletal survey).
Attitudes: Recognize the impact of the disease on the child and family; demonstrate empathy and sympathy to parents; offer support as needed; maintain confidentiality.

topics.title: Approach to a child with cyanotic heart disease
objectives: Goals: Obtain a detailed history of a child presenting with cyanosis; understand the etiological and pathophysiological differences between central and peripheral cyanosis; recognize signs and symptoms of systemic diseases causing cyanosis at different age groups; differentiate cardiac, respiratory, central and other causes of cyanosis; list possible differential diagnoses and a stepwise approach for assessment of each of the common conditions; interpret the results of the ECG and x-ray; recognize common cardiac conditions in children presenting with cyanosis as per age of presentation; know the complications associated with central causes of cyanosis (paradoxical emboli, arrhythmias, brain abscess and infarction, thrombus formation in the heart, pneumothorax, bronchiectasis); understand the mechanism of action of drugs/surgery in the treatment of these diseases; understand the management of acute cyanotic spells in children; counsel the families accordingly.

Knowledge: Define, describe, and discuss causes of cyanosis in neonates, infants, and children including understanding duct-dependent pulmonary circulation and the importance of prostaglandin to maintain duct patency - neonatal: congenital cyanotic heart diseases with intracardiac mixing/right-to-left shunt (tetralogy of Fallot, transposition of great arteries, total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage, tricuspid atresia, truncus arteriosus, single ventricle lesions); with decreased pulmonary blood flow (pulmonary atresia/critical PS, tetralogy of Fallot, Ebstein's anomaly, Fallot's physiology disorders); respiratory causes (RDS, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, congenital lobar emphysema, CCAM, pneumonia, sepsis); central causes (asphyxia, maternal sedatives, intracranial hemorrhage, hypoglycemia, disordered control of breathing - central apnea, Ondine's curse); other disorders (physiologic acrocyanosis, sepsis, shock). Infant and child: cardiac (congenital cyanotic heart diseases - tetralogy of Fallot, Fallot's physiology disorders, complex cardiac lesions post palliative surgeries - BT shunt, Glenn, Fontan); peripheral cyanosis due to poor perfusion (cardiogenic shock, CCF, arrhythmias, cardiomyopathies, myocarditis); respiratory (chronic lung disease, severe asthma, cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, foreign body); CNS (prolonged seizures, disordered control of breathing, central apnea); peripheral (vascular problems, polycythemia, peripheral hypoxia, obstruction - superior vena cava syndrome, deep vein thrombosis).

History taking: Elicit a detailed history of the cyanotic episode including onset, course, duration, aggravating and relieving factors, recurrence, sites, mucosal involvement, response to crying and to oxygen; the nature of cyanosis (central or peripheral or both) helps decide severity; elicit history of associated symptoms (breathlessness, palpitations, chest pain, syncope, squatting episodes, loss of consciousness, seizures, easy fatigability, lethargy); elicit history of previous similar episodes; elicit history of previous surgeries (BT shunt, septostomy, Glenn, Fontan); elicit history to differentiate other causes of cyanosis (respiratory, CNS, peripheral); elicit detailed prenatal history (maternal sedation, prolonged labor, traumatic delivery, setup for sepsis); elicit detailed history of maternal DM, SLE, drug intake (phenytoin, warfarin, valproate, lithium), maternal infections (TORCH, syphilis), maternal antenatal scan results; elicit detailed family history (consanguinity, congenital heart disease, respiratory or central issues, sudden young unexplained death); elicit drug history for aspirin and oral or injectable anticoagulants.

Physical examination: Perform a detailed cardio-respiratory physical examination; general examination (cyanosis, clubbing, pallor - know where to look for central and peripheral cyanosis and understand differential and reverse differential cyanosis); measurement of blood pressures in 4 limbs, pre- and post-ductal SpO2, respiratory and heart rate; assess for respiratory distress (suprasternal, subcostal, intercostal recessions, nasal flare); evaluate for precordial prominence (right vs left ventricular impulses, hyperdynamic chest wall, palpable thrills and heaves); assess and analyze 1st and 2nd heart sounds and understand S3 and S4; assess for murmurs in different areas; differentiate systolic and diastolic murmurs; differentiate holosystolic, long systolic, and ejection systolic murmurs; assess for signs of cardiac failure (basal creps, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, JVP in older children); assess for dysmorphic features of syndromes like trisomy 21 and Turner syndrome; perform a detailed systemic examination to differentiate other causes of cyanosis.

Differential diagnosis: Based on history and physical examination, list differential diagnoses - congenital cyanotic heart diseases (TOF, transposition of great arteries, Ebstein's anomaly, pulmonary atresia, total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage, persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn); respiratory disorders (respiratory distress syndrome, sepsis and pneumonia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, other congenital lung anomalies); central disorders (birth asphyxia, seizures, intraventricular hemorrhage).

Laboratory interpretation: Select and interpret laboratory investigations including: hyperoxia test; arterial blood gases; full blood counts; CRP; blood C&S; random blood glucose; cranial ultrasound; chest X-ray; 12-lead ECG.
Basic procedural skills: Observe 12-lead ECG; blood pressure and SpO2 measurement upper and lower limbs; arterial blood gas; 2-D echocardiogram.

Communication skills: Discuss and communicate to the parents regarding the nature, cause and seriousness of the disease; explain what is duct-dependent pulmonary circulation and the importance of keeping the duct open; explain the plans for treatment of the disease; educate and counsel the parents and family about the possible present means of treatment and different factors responsible for the situation; explain the possible complications of the disease if left untreated.

Management: Design an appropriate treatment plan for congenital cyanotic heart diseases; understand the importance of keeping the duct open in duct-dependent pulmonary circulations and select appropriate drugs such as prostaglandins for ductal patency (e.g. transposition of great vessels, pulmonary atresia, Ebstein's anomaly).
Attitudes: Demonstrate a professional attitude of commitment and honesty towards long-term management of diseases like congenital heart diseases and chronic lung disorders.

topics.title: Approach to a child with a murmur
objectives: Goals: Obtain a detailed history of a child presenting with a murmur or suspected cardiogenic shock; recognize 'innocent' murmurs and differentiate them from pathological murmurs; understand the etiology and pathophysiology of different pathological murmurs; recognize the signs and symptoms of common congenital heart diseases presenting with a murmur or cardiogenic shock; recognize common cardiac conditions in children presenting with cardiogenic shock as per age of presentation; recognize common cardiac conditions presenting at different ages with a murmur; list possible differential diagnoses and a stepwise approach for assessment of each of the common conditions; interpret the results of the ECG and x-ray; know possible complications associated with CHD; understand the role of drugs/surgery in the treatment of CHD; management of duct-dependent systemic circulation.

Knowledge: Define, describe, and discuss causes of murmurs and presentations with cardiogenic shock in neonates, infants and children; understand duct-dependent systemic circulation and the importance of prostaglandin to maintain duct patency - neonatal: congenital acyanotic heart diseases with a murmur (VSD, AVSD, PDA, aortic stenosis, pulmonary stenosis, ASD); with cardiogenic shock (coarctation of aorta, aortic atresia/critical AS, interrupted aortic arch, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, Shone's complex); innocent murmurs in the neonate (closing ductus arteriosus, peripheral pulmonary stenosis). Infant and child: benign or innocent murmurs (Still's murmur, hemic murmur, aortic and pulmonary flow murmurs, venous hum); pathological murmurs (ASD, pulmonary stenosis, aortic stenosis, VSD, PDA, mitral regurgitation, aortic regurgitation).

History taking: Elicit a detailed history of the presenting or referring complaint including when the murmur was first noticed, whether it has progressed or resolved, duration, any factors associated with the finding (URI or vaccine check); elicit history of associated symptoms (breathlessness with feeding, sweating with feeds, interrupted feeds, poor weight gain, chest retractions); in older children also dyspnea on exertion, palpitations, chest pain, syncope, loss of consciousness, easy fatigability and lethargy; elicit detailed prenatal history (maternal sedation, prolonged labor, traumatic delivery, setup for sepsis); elicit detailed history of maternal DM, SLE, drug intake (phenytoin, warfarin, valproate, lithium), maternal infections (TORCH, syphilis), maternal antenatal scan results; elicit detailed family history (consanguinity, congenital heart disease, respiratory or central issues, sudden young unexplained death); for a child presenting in shock, identify the type of shock and, in case of cardiogenic shock, the most likely cause.

Physical examination: Perform a detailed cardio-respiratory physical examination; general examination (cyanosis, clubbing, pallor, icterus, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum); measurement of blood pressures in 4 limbs, pre- and post-ductal SpO2, respiratory and heart rate, assessment of JVP; assess for respiratory distress (suprasternal, subcostal, intercostal recessions, nasal flare, Harrison's sulcus); evaluate for precordial prominence (right vs left ventricular impulses, hyperdynamic chest wall, palpable thrills and heaves); assess and analyze 1st and 2nd heart sounds and understand S3 and S4; assess for murmurs in different areas; differentiate systolic and diastolic murmurs; differentiate holosystolic, long systolic, and ejection systolic murmurs; assess for signs of cardiac failure (basal crepts, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, JVP); assess for dysmorphic features of syndromes like trisomy 21 and Turner syndrome; know the differences between streptococcal vs viral pharyngitis.
Differential diagnosis: Based on history and physical examination, list differential diagnoses: causes of murmur; cardiogenic shock; benign and innocent murmurs.
Laboratory interpretation: Select and interpret laboratory investigations.
Basic procedural skills: Observe throat swab collection.

Communication skills: Discuss and communicate to the parents regarding the nature, cause and seriousness of the disease; explain what is duct-dependent systemic circulation and the importance of keeping the duct open; explain the future plans for treatment; educate and counsel the parents and family about present means of treatment and factors responsible; explain the possible complications of the disease if left untreated.

Management: Design an appropriate treatment plan for congenital acyanotic heart diseases; understand the importance of keeping the duct open in duct-dependent systemic circulation and select appropriate drugs such as prostaglandins for ductal patency (coarctation of the aorta, interrupted aortic arch, aortic atresia, hypoplastic left heart syndrome); understand the basis and know the management of common acyanotic heart diseases; identify the possible associations and complications of congenital heart disease (congestive cardiac failure, paradoxical embolism, brain abscess, stroke, pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary hypertensive crises, infective endocarditis, Eisenmenger syndrome, arrhythmias, failure to thrive, recurrent infections).

Attitudes: Understand the mental stress and anxiety related to the disease process in parents and family; demonstrate a professional attitude of commitment and honesty towards long-term management of diseases like congenital heart diseases and chronic lung disorders.

topics.title: Approach to common infections in children
objectives: Goals: Describe the age-related occurrence and clinical presentation of upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs), acute otitis media (AOM) and urinary tract infection (UTI) in children; formulate management plans for URTIs, AOM and UTI; describe the main recognized complications of UTI, streptococcal pharyngitis, and AOM.
Knowledge: Classification & clinical presentation of URTIs (common cold, AOM, sinusitis, pharyngitis & tonsillitis) and AOM.
Knowledge: Clinical differentiation between streptococcal and viral pharyngitis.
Knowledge: Classification of UTI: clinically (asymptomatic versus symptomatic) and anatomically (cystitis versus pyelonephritis).
Knowledge: Choice of urine collection (e.g. mid-stream & catheterized specimen).
Knowledge: List of likely causative pathogens for common infections in children.
Knowledge: Pathogenesis of common infections in children.
Knowledge: Workup and management of URTIs & AOM.
Knowledge: Predisposing factors for UTI.
Knowledge: Workup and management of UTI.
Knowledge: Interventions to control transmission and enhance prevention of URTIs & AOM (immunization against specific pathogens and infection control measures).
Knowledge: Complications of Group A streptococcal pharyngitis (suppurative and non-suppurative).
Knowledge: Recognized complications of AOM and UTI.

History taking: Identify and describe symptoms of presenting complaint (onset, duration, aggravating and relieving factors); general (fever, headache, fatigue, cough, vomiting, poor oral intake); ears (tugging, discharge, pain); nose (runny nose, nasal blockage, sneezing); eyes (tearing, discharge, burning, itching, redness); throat (sore throat, scratchy throat, bad breath, hoarseness); urinary symptoms (dysuria, offensive urine, suprapubic pain, loin pain); other voiding history (frequency, urgency, stream, volume, secondary enuresis, toileting practices); risk factors for the infection (e.g. constipation in UTI); previous similar episodes; medication history; immunization history; relevant family history (e.g. urological abnormalities for UTI); relevant social history.

Physical examination: General appearance; vital signs (hypertension should raise suspicion of hydronephrosis or renal parenchymal disease); hydration status; inconsolability; snoring, rhinorrhea, mouth breathing; throat (tonsillar enlargement, erythema, edema, exudate, vesicles, ulceration); ear (otorrhea, erythema and/or bulging tympanic membrane); abdomen (palpable bladder, dribbling or straining, costovertebral angle or suprapubic tenderness); look for underlying conditions that contribute to infections (e.g. spina bifida for UTI); other relevant systemic examination.

Laboratory interpretation: Based on the clinical assessment: complete blood count with differential; inflammatory markers; rapid antigen detection test (RADT) for streptococcal pharyngitis; throat swab culture; respiratory viral panel PCR; urine dipstick/urinalysis; urine microscopy and culture; blood culture; urea, creatinine & electrolytes; renal ultrasound; voiding cystourethrography (VCUG).
Basic procedural skills: Nasopharyngeal swab/aspiration; suction (nasal/oral); urinary catheterization; urine dipstick test.

Communication skills: Address, incorporate and respond to parental concerns; deliver well-explained and positive management recommendations to increase parental understanding and acceptance of non-antibiotic therapy in viral URTIs.
Management: Management of URTIs & AOM; management of UTI.

Attitudes: Achieve and maintain appropriate infection prevention and control practice; understand the concept and function of a multidisciplinary team (e.g. managing recurrent UTI: general pediatrics, nephrology, urology & infectious diseases specialties).

topics.title: Approach to prolonged fever in children
objectives: Goals: Define fever of unknown origin and differentiate from other prolonged or recurrent fevers; understand the common causes of fever of unknown origin and develop a systematic approach to diagnosis and management; gain a basic understanding of periodic fever syndromes in children.
Knowledge: Definition of fever in children.
Knowledge: Definition of fever of unknown origin.
Knowledge: Subtypes of fever of unknown origin.
Knowledge: Identification of other prolonged or recurrent fever patterns.
Knowledge: Differential diagnosis of fever of unknown origin (infectious, inflammatory/autoimmune, neoplastic, other).
Knowledge: A general approach to fever of unknown origin.
Knowledge: Specific findings on history and examination that point to common etiologies of FUO.
Knowledge: Neutropenic and nosocomial FUO.
Knowledge: Periodic fever syndromes in children.

History taking: Age at onset (determine if the cause is hereditary); measurement technique; height of fever, duration, pattern, association with sweats or chills; predictability of pattern; fever with headaches, sinus pressure, blocked nose (sinusitis); respiratory symptoms (pneumonia); mucosal changes, conjunctivitis, rash (Kawasaki); fatigue, swollen lymph nodes (EBV); fatigue, bruising, bleeding, weight loss, swollen lymph nodes (leukemia, lymphoma); abnormal eye movements, diarrhea, raccoon eyes (neuroblastoma); abdominal discomfort (abscess); weight loss, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea (inflammatory bowel disease); musculoskeletal complaints (osteomyelitis); rash and arthritis (rheumatic fever, JIA); nervousness, tachycardia, tremors, heat intolerance (hyperthyroidism); travel (tuberculosis, malaria, typhoid); history of cardiac anomaly/surgery (endocarditis); hospital stay or medical devices (nosocomial); neutropenia/immunodeficiency (neutropenic fever); animal exposure (cat scratch disease, brucellosis, Q fever, salmonella); food exposure, unpasteurized dairy, undercooked meat (brucellosis, Q fever, salmonella, toxoplasmosis); family history of autoimmune or autoinflammatory disease, consanguinity; medication exposure (drug fever); inconsistent history by parents, history of abuse or neglect (Munchausen by proxy).

Physical examination: Correct measurement of core body temperature; vital signs, height, weight (growth chart); general (cachexia, mental status); HEENT (retina, conjunctivae, tympanic membranes, sinuses, mouth and throat, lymph nodes); chest (tachypnea, abnormal breath sounds, clubbing); heart (tachycardia, murmurs, stigmata of endocarditis); GI (hepatosplenomegaly, masses, rectal tag); skin (rash, bruises, petechiae); skeletal (bone or joint abnormalities); lymphadenopathy; neurologic (mental status, CNs, opsoclonus-myoclonus, meningeal signs, gait); hospitalized patients: medical devices.

Laboratory interpretation: Know how to prioritize: review previous results; CBC with peripheral smear; U&E, bone profile; LFTs; ESR and CRPs; urinalysis, urine culture; blood culture; chest x-ray; targeted investigations based on findings on history and examination.
Basic procedural skills: Measuring temperature.

Communication skills: Elicit a detailed history from the family to identify potential causes; counsel the family about the possible diagnoses and process of investigations, being comfortable with the uncertainty surrounding these cases in the initial stages; be able to gain the confidence of the family despite not having a clear diagnosis initially.

Management: Thorough history and examination, basic investigations, targeted studies; prioritizing investigations, beginning with more common causes then less common causes (stepwise approach); maintaining a diary of fevers and symptoms; repeat visits; a systematic approach to differential diagnosis (infectious, autoimmune, malignancy, others).

Attitudes: Understand that it may take several visits and a sequence of investigations to identify the cause; work professionally in a multidisciplinary team including nursing, laboratories, radiologists, pulmonologists; maintain good infection control practices when an infection is suspected.

topics.title: Approach to proteinuria in children
objectives: Goals: Recognize that proteinuria can be symptomatic or asymptomatic; recognize the need to include urinalysis in the physical examination of children; differentiate between transient and persistent proteinuria and between glomerular and tubular proteinuria; list the important investigations needed to reach the diagnosis; know that the treatment of proteinuria depends on the etiology.

Knowledge: Define proteinuria by the 3 different methods: the dipstick, spot urine sample for protein to creatinine ratio, and the 24-hour collection of urinary protein; know that the urinary dipstick is a screening tool and needs to be confirmed by urinary protein to creatinine ratio and the gold standard 24-hour urinary collection; list the different reasons for false positive and false negative proteinuria on the dipstick.

Knowledge: Normal protein excretion in children is defined as negative or trace on urine dipstick, protein to creatinine ratio of less than 20 mg/mmol (less than 60 mg/mmol in children less than 2 years), and 24-hour protein excretion of less than or equal to 4 mg/m2/hour.

Knowledge: Abnormal protein excretion in children is defined as more than or equal to 1+ on urine dipstick, protein to creatinine ratio of more than 20 mg/mmol (more than 60 mg/mmol in children less than 2 years), and 24-hour protein excretion of more than 4 mg/m2/hour.

Knowledge: Nephrotic range proteinuria in children is defined as more than or equal to +2-3 on urine dipstick, protein to creatinine ratio of more than 250 mg/mmol, and 24-hour protein excretion of 40 mg/m2/hour.
Knowledge: Know how to classify the different causes of proteinuria: intermittent (non-postural and postural) and persistent (glomerular and tubular).
Knowledge: Exclude orthostatic proteinuria, defined as early morning urine samples (supine) negative for protein while evening urine samples (upright) may contain varying concentrations of protein.
Knowledge: Know the typical example of transient/benign proteinuria in the neonatal period: the Tamm-Horsfall protein that accounts for higher levels of protein excretion in this age group.

History taking: Obtain a detailed history to identify the etiology of proteinuria (transient, orthostatic or persistent); symptoms of renal failure or glomerulonephritis (edema, hematuria, oliguria); symptoms of connective tissue diseases (joint pains and rashes); symptoms of recurrent urinary tract infections may suggest reflux nephropathy; medications history including NSAIDs; family history of polycystic kidney disease, renal failure, dialysis, renal transplant, or deafness.

Physical examination: Evidence of chronic kidney disease such as failure to thrive, anemia, and renal osteodystrophy; blood pressure measured with the proper cuff according to age and size of the child (hypertension might indicate underlying renal disease); look for clues of fluid overload (raised JVP, hepatomegaly, edema, reduced air entry at lung bases, ascites, scrotal or labial edema - seen in nephritic and nephrotic syndromes); look for signs of systemic illnesses (palpable rash on extensor surfaces of lower limbs suggesting Henoch-Schoenlein; joint swelling and erythema suggesting connective tissue disorders); palpable flank masses might suggest polycystic kidney disease or hydronephrosis.

Differential diagnosis: List different causes of proteinuria - intermittent non-postural proteinuria (fever, exercise, dehydration, stress); intermittent postural proteinuria (orthostatic proteinuria); persistent glomerular proteinuria (primary glomerulonephropathies e.g. minimal change disease and focal segmental glomerulonephritis; secondary glomerulonephropathies e.g. postinfectious glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, IgA nephropathy); persistent tubular proteinuria (hereditary e.g. all causes of Fanconi syndrome such as cystinosis, galactosemia, tyrosinemia; acquired e.g. interstitial nephritis and pyelonephritis).

Laboratory interpretation (symptomatic): Recognize that detailed investigations should be started early for children with symptoms suggestive of renal disease; list investigations including urine microscopy and culture, urine protein to creatinine ratio and 24-hr urine protein collection, complete blood count, serum urea, creatinine, electrolytes, albumin, total cholesterol, ASO titer, complements C3, C4, IgA, ANA, ds-DNA, ANCA, Hepatitis C, B, and renal ultrasound; know that renal biopsy is indicated in persistent significant unexplained proteinuria, associated hematuria, persistent complement abnormalities, evidence of connective tissue disease.

Laboratory interpretation (asymptomatic): Know that 3-6 months follow-up is required in this group until urine dipstick is negative; know that investigations done for symptomatic proteinuria will need to be done if the proteinuria persists, if hematuria develops, and if proteinuria worsens.

Basic procedural skills: Observe measuring blood pressure using the proper sized cuff according to child age and size; performing urine dipstick and interpreting the result; collecting blood for lab tests.

Communication skills: With colleagues and nurses regarding the investigations, treatment and follow-up plan; with the parents to discuss possible causes and expected complications; counsel and educate parents about the required workup and treatment plans.

Management: Assessment of the child with proteinuria; proper workup and follow-up; identifying the underlying cause to offer the proper treatment; refer to the subspecialty concerned after identifying the cause; interpret laboratory investigation results in relation to the etiology.
Attitudes: Diligent perseverance in ascertaining cause of proteinuria; counseling parents regarding possible etiologies and management plan.

topics.title: Approach to a child with hematuria
objectives: Goals: Learn a comprehensive approach to a child with hematuria; avoid unnecessary and extensive workup for hematuria due to benign condition; identify those cases of hematuria that need advanced investigation and specific treatment; know when to refer these cases to a pediatric nephrologist.
Knowledge: Define hematuria - gross hematuria is visible dark urine; microscopic hematuria is defined as the presence of at least 5 red blood cells (RBC) per microliter of urine.
Knowledge: Be aware of causes of dark or red colored urine that are not due to the presence of RBC (false positive hematuria) like certain foods, drugs, hemoglobinuria, and myoglobinuria.

Knowledge: Know that in a child with dark urine due to drugs or foods the urine dipstick will be negative for blood, and in a child with dark urine due to hemoglobinuria and myoglobinuria the urine dipstick will be positive for blood but urine microscopy will not show the presence of RBCs.

Knowledge: Know that hematuria may originate from any site in the urinary system (glomeruli, renal tubules, ureters, urinary bladder, urethra); hematuria can be glomerular or non-glomerular in origin.
Knowledge: Know the differential diagnosis for glomerular and non-glomerular origin hematuria.
Knowledge: Understand the pathophysiology of hematuria due to glomerular and non-glomerular origin and their specific clinical presentation, workup, and treatment.

History taking: Take a proper history to describe the hematuria as gross or microscopic and intermittent or persistent; identify whether hematuria is initial (beginning of micturition only), total (throughout micturition) or terminal (at the end of micturition) as it may help determine the cause and sites of bleeding; take a detailed history of medications, recent foods, any chronic hematological illness with chronic hemolysis or any history of muscle pain and tenderness to rule out false-positive causes; recent history of trauma or strenuous exercise or chronic coagulopathy; abdominal or flank pain and history of stone passage to rule out renal stone disease; history of upper respiratory tract illness before onset of hematuria to rule out acute glomerulonephritis or IgA nephropathy; symptoms of systemic connective tissue disorders (oral ulcers, joint pains, skin rash); history of dysuria, urgency, frequency, fever and flank pain to rule out UTI; family history of renal disease with deafness (Alport's syndrome) or family history of hematuria without deafness or renal failure (benign familial hematuria).

Physical examination: Look for the presence of hypertension and edema which points towards acute glomerulonephritis; check for skin rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, joint swelling or tenderness (systemic lupus erythematosus or Henoch-Schoenlein purpura); look for signs of volume overload (raised JVP, edema, decreased air entry at lung bases, hepatomegaly, ascites) suggestive of renal failure due to glomerulonephritis; abdominal examination to look for palpable kidneys (gross hydronephrosis, polycystic kidney disease, renal tumors); check for costovertebral angle tenderness or suprapubic tenderness suggestive of pyelonephritis or cystitis respectively.

Differential diagnosis: Causes of glomerular hematuria: acute post-infectious glomerulonephritis, chronic glomerulonephritis, inherited nephropathies, systemic disorders. Causes of non-glomerular hematuria.

Laboratory interpretation: Decide what tests are needed for evaluation and prioritize the urgency of the tests accordingly: complete blood count; urea creatinine electrolytes; urinary microscopy and urinary culture; urine protein to creatinine ratio; urine calcium to creatinine ratio; ASO titer, complements C3, C4, IgA, ANA, ds-DNA, ANCA, Hepatitis B and C; abdominal ultrasound; renal biopsy; CT scan abdomen for renal masses or stones; cystoscopy.

Basic procedural skills: Observe measuring blood pressure using the proper sized cuff according to child age and proper method of applying the BP cuff; plotting the observed BP reading on standard BP percentile charts for gender, age, and height; collecting blood for lab tests; performing the urine dipstick test and its interpretation; observe percutaneous renal biopsy.

Communication skills: With colleagues and nurses regarding the investigations, treatment, and follow-up plan; with the parents to discuss possible causes and expected complications; counsel and educate parents about the required workup and treatment plans.

Management: Assessment of a child with hematuria; proper and judicious work-up, avoiding unnecessary investigation in benign cases and at the same time identifying those who need urgent attention and extensive workup; identifying the underlying cause to offer the proper treatment; refer to the subspecialty concerned after identifying the cause.
Attitudes: Diligent perseverance in ascertaining the cause; counseling parents regarding outcome both short and long term.

topics.title: Approach to global developmental delay and intellectual disability
objectives: Knowledge: Define and describe typical child neurodevelopment during different periods of development.
Knowledge: Differentiate between child growth and child development.
Knowledge: Recognize the importance of early care of child development (critical period of human brain development).
Knowledge: Define developmental delay, global developmental delay/intellectual disability.
Knowledge: Identify conditions that can result in global developmental delay.
Knowledge: Discuss the causes of speech delay.
Knowledge: Discuss causes of motor delay (Duchenne disease, cerebral palsy).
Knowledge: Discuss psychometric tools to assess development, such as developmental screening and IQ tests.
Knowledge: Describe the multidisciplinary management of a child with developmental delay.

History taking: Obtain a complete pediatric medical and psychosocial history; obtain detailed developmental milestones history; differentiate static developmental delay, progressive delay and neuroregression; obtain history focusing on possible etiological factors such as perinatal events, genetic and environmental causes; obtain history of medical, behavioral and other neurodevelopmental health conditions.

Physical examination: Perform a complete pediatric physical examination including neurological examination; identify any neuro-cutaneous marker or dysmorphic features; perform hearing and visual assessment.
Developmental screening: Assess the current developmental level; perform developmental screening.

Laboratory interpretation: Select appropriate diagnostic and laboratory tests (there is no single diagnostic workup appropriate to all cases) including: basic blood investigations (CBC, iron studies, lead level); metabolic screening; thyroid function tests, creatinine kinase (CK), TORCH; molecular genetic tests (microarray CGH, whole-exome sequencing, Fragile X); radiologic imaging of the brain; neuro-physiological studies (e.g. EEG, audiometry, VEP, EMG).

Communication skills: Observe and practice counseling skills to educate parents and patient about the condition; explain the developmental stimulation program; discuss the importance of multidisciplinary approach including speech and language therapy as well as community services available for children with special needs.

Management: Design an appropriate evaluation and treatment plan for patients including: referral to different pediatric subspecialties for detailed evaluation by a multidisciplinary team; referral to community services available for the care of developmentally challenged children; provide resources for parent-mediated developmental stimulation program.

Attitudes: Demonstrate the ability to assess the age-related developmental milestones; use cost-effective considerations in the selection of appropriate laboratory tests if needed; understand the impact of caring for a child with developmental delay on the family; recommend family support through available resources; inform about the local and online available resources for rehabilitation; interact with other professionals involved in patient care through effective teamwork.

topics.title: Approach to common neurodevelopmental disorders in children (ASD)
objectives: Knowledge: Define Autism spectrum disorder.
Knowledge: Discuss the clinical manifestations of ASD.
Knowledge: Discuss the diagnostic criteria included in the diagnosis of ASD.
Knowledge: Propose a differential diagnosis list in a child with disruptive behavior.
Knowledge: List the important co-morbidities associated with ASD.
Knowledge: Understand the impact of ASD on family life.
Knowledge: Discuss different intervention modalities for managing ASD.
Knowledge: Discuss the role of any pharmacological agents used in the management of ASD.

Screening: Recognize the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers (M-CHAT/R) as a helpful tool to screen for autism in children between ages 16 and 30 months; in Oman, M-CHAT/R screening is integrated within the Extended Program of Immunization service in all Primary Health Care institutions at age 18 months.

History taking: Perform a complete history in regards to ASD in different age groups (both younger and older children); this includes interviews regarding birth, early development and family history, history of social-emotional interaction and verbal and non-verbal communicative behaviors, daily functioning, any gastrointestinal problem and sleep issue; identify stereotypic/repetitive behaviors, any rituals or rigidity and any sensory sensitivity in history or on clinical observation.
Physical examination: Perform a complete physical examination including neurological examination; check growth parameters and identify distinctive facial features and/or neurocutaneous markers.

Laboratory interpretation: Recognize that ASD is a clinical diagnosis; propose appropriate investigations in a child with ASD if indicated such as: tests for vision and hearing; blood tests for TFT, metabolic screening, lead level and molecular genetic testing; MRI brain.

Communication skills: Communicate effectively with patients and their families to enable them to undertake decisions as equal partners; provide the list of rehabilitation resources available in the community; communicate effectively with colleagues, faculty, and the community to improve the care of children with ASD; interact with other professionals involved in patient care through effective teamwork.
Management: Design an appropriate evaluation and treatment plan for children with ASD; discuss the behavioral and any pharmacological treatment in ASD.

Attitudes: Demonstrate the ability to assess efficiently children with ASD; demonstrate the ability to develop long-term follow-up plans with families of affected children, as it affects the schooling and social life.

topics.title: Approach to the child with abdominal pain
objectives: Goals: Define acute and chronic abdominal pain and identify important aspects in history and physical examination; describe organic and functional causes of acute and chronic abdominal pain; recognize medical and surgical causes of abdominal pain; formulate a management plan for children with acute and chronic abdominal pain, and know when to refer to different specialists.
Knowledge: Discuss common causes of acute and chronic abdominal pain in infants and children.
Knowledge: Describe symptoms and signs associated with common surgical causes of acute abdominal pain such as: incarcerated hernia, intussusception, acute appendicitis.

Knowledge: Describe symptoms and signs associated with common medical causes of abdominal pain, acute and chronic, such as: constipation (describe soiling and encopresis), acute gastroenteritis, mesenteric lymphadenitis, gastritis and gastric ulcer, peritonitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis, acute pyelonephritis/renal colic, lower lobe pneumonia/pharyngitis, VOC in sickle cell disease, diabetic ketoacidosis.
Knowledge: Describe symptoms and signs associated with other conditions that may precipitate abdominal pain.
Knowledge: Identify the difference between organic and functional abdominal pain.
Knowledge: Identify the red flags in chronic abdominal pain.

History taking: Demonstrate clear history taking that will differentiate etiology of the disease; define the severity and characteristic of abdominal pain; identify symptoms associated with abdominal pain (vomiting, diarrhea, tenesmus, loss of appetite, jaundice, loss of weight, constipation, PR bleeding, nocturnal stools, passage of meconium in neonatal period); relate the character of abdominal pain to different etiologies (epigastric pain of gastritis; pain radiating to the back in acute pancreatitis; right hypochondriac pain in hepatitis/cholecystitis; left iliac fossa pain in constipation/ulcerative colitis); identify red flags in child with chronic abdominal pain; identify psychological and social stressors; identify the family history of GI disorder; identify the history of drug ingestion.

Physical examination: Perform a thorough physical examination to establish the diagnosis and severity of abdominal pain; recognize and correlate abnormal behavior of a sick infant or child (lethargy, weak cry, episodic bouts of screaming); recognize the importance of detection of abnormal vital signs; relate the signs to different etiological factors.

Differential diagnosis: Formulate a differential diagnosis for acute abdominal pain in children; formulate a differential diagnosis for chronic abdominal pain in children including organic and functional pain.

Laboratory interpretation: Propose appropriate diagnostic and laboratory tests for a child with acute abdominal pain; propose appropriate diagnostic and laboratory tests for a child with chronic abdominal pain; interpret the results of diagnostic tests used in a child with abdominal pain; laboratory and diagnostic tests when appropriate should include hematological, biochemical, microbiological, radiology tests, manometry for achalasia or constipation, endoscopy in gastritis, gastric ulcer or inflammatory bowel diseases.
Basic procedural skills: Insertion of a nasogastric tube.

Communication skills: Communicate and establish rapport with the child and his family; explain the etiology and its pathophysiology to the child/his family; explain specific treatment plans for the child/family.
Management: Design an appropriate evaluation and treatment plan including recognition of ileus/intestinal obstruction and perforation in intestinal obstruction.

Attitudes: Listen attentively to elicit and synthesize relevant information to the patient's illness; recognize the psychosocial effect of the illness on the child and his family; communicate effectively with colleagues, faculty, and patients; interact with other professionals involved in patient care through effective teamwork.

Clinical tutorial learning objectives: Differentiate between different types of abdominal pain; distinguish functional from organic abdominal pain; discuss common etiologies of abdominal pain (both acute and chronic) in children; recognize surgical and medical causes of acute abdominal pain; identify the important points of history and physical examination in a child with acute abdominal pain; describe the causes of chronic abdominal pain; distinguish chronic functional from chronic organic abdominal pain; identify red flags in a child with chronic abdominal pain and their relation to certain conditions; discuss the functional and organic causes of chronic constipation.

topics.title: Approach to a child with diarrhea (acute & chronic)
objectives: Goals: Recognize signs and symptoms of acute and chronic diarrhea of varied etiology in all age groups and provide optimum treatment.
Knowledge: Define acute and chronic diarrhea and differentiate secretory vs osmotic diarrhea.
Knowledge: Recognize etiology, pathogenesis and clinical features of infective diarrhea including gastroenteritis (rotavirus, Norwalk, adenovirus, influenza, enterovirus).
Knowledge: Recognize etiology, pathogenesis, and clinical features of diarrhea caused by malabsorption.
Knowledge: Recognize etiology, pathogenesis, and clinical features of diarrhea in the neonatal period.
Knowledge: Recognize etiology, pathogenesis, and clinical features of diarrhea caused by other causes.
Knowledge: Signs of dehydration (mild, moderate, severe).
Knowledge: Types of dehydration (hypo/hypernatremic dehydration).
Knowledge: Management of dehydration and associated metabolic derangements in the acute stage.
Knowledge: Management of specific causes of chronic diarrhea.
Knowledge: Long-term complications of diarrheal diseases.

History taking: Obtain a detailed history of nature and type of diarrhea; obtain a detailed history of duration of diarrhea and associated etiology of chronic causes of diarrhea; obtain nutritional history including details of the introduction of a weaning diet; obtain history suggestive of food poisoning; clarify any recent history of travel; family history of a similar problem; vaccination and drug history.

Physical examination: Assessment of pulse (rate, volume, peripheral pulses), capillary refill time, monitoring blood pressure, skin (mottling, temperature); assess severity of diarrhea and chronicity (failure to thrive, associated features of chronic chest problem such as clubbing as in cystic fibrosis); assess dehydration and features of electrolyte imbalances; skin and oral mucosa examination looking for extraintestinal features of chronic diarrhea; abdominal examination including inspection for abdominal distention or obvious mass, palpation for tenderness, masses or organomegaly, auscultation; systemic examination to identify features of diseases causing chronic diarrhea.
