Laboratory interpretation: Select basic investigations for acute and chronic diarrhea which may include: full blood count; electrolytes and renal function (to identify hypo-, hyper- or isonatremic dehydration, acidosis, prerenal azotemia); stool culture and viral studies; in case of chronic diarrhea, stool for reducing substances, stool pH, special investigations for celiac disease (anti-endomysial, anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies, jejunal biopsy if needed), cystic fibrosis (sweat test, fecal elastase), immunodeficiency, if indicated; radiological studies if indicated (barium swallow and follow-through in case of malrotation, blind loop); endoscopic examinations (celiac disease, inflammatory bowel diseases); interpret electrolyte imbalances and metabolic derangements following diarrheal diseases.
Basic procedural skills: Intravenous access; nasogastric insertion; venesection for blood sampling.

Communication skills: Discuss with parents about oral rehydration therapy; educate parents about early recognition of dehydration; discuss with parents about the prevention of diarrheal diseases; counsel regarding the etiology of chronic diarrheal illness and long-term prognosis.

Management: Assess hydration status of a child effectively; recommend oral rehydration therapy and intravenous fluid therapy correctly; recognize and manage hypovolaemic shock; recognize and manage electrolyte imbalances and metabolic acidosis; recommend appropriate antibiotic treatment of infective diarrhea; recommend specific treatment of causes of chronic diarrhea (coeliac disease, IBD); recommend replacement of nutritional deficiencies; refer to a pediatric gastroenterologist when indicated.

Attitudes: Demonstrate urgency in managing severely dehydrated children; allay anxiety of parents; realize the importance of constantly communicating with the parents about progress in the treatment of sick children.

general_objectives: Apply the knowledge gained in basic science such as anatomy, physiology, biochemistry when performing and interpreting the procedures in clinical practice.
Understand the indications and contraindications of commonly performed bedside procedures.
Acquire the necessary skills to perform the common bedside procedures performed in clinical encounters with a patient.
Demonstrate ability to safely perform the common bedside procedures.
Apply the principles of medical ethics, professionalism and patient safety in clinical practice.
Incorporate evidence-based medicine as a means of lifelong learning in clinical practice.

topics.title: Airway station
objectives: Orient students to basic airway management skills.
Set of maneuvers to prevent and relieve airway obstruction.
Identify advantages and disadvantages of various devices for airway management.
Issues related to aspiration and prevention.

Identify indications for intubation and prepare necessary equipment including: bag and mask ventilation; triple manoeuvre (head tilt, chin lift and jaw thrust); insertion of oral and nasal airway; insertion of laryngeal mask airway; endotracheal tube insertion and confirmation.

topics.title: Knotting, suturing and suture removal
objectives: To know the basic instruments required for suturing and how to handle them: tissue forceps (toothed, non-toothed), artery forceps (curved, straight), needle holder, scissors (curved and straight).
To know the universal precautions to handle sharp instruments.
To know different types of needles and suture materials.
To get basic practical orientation in doing interrupted and continuous suturing in the given suture pad.
To know the use of scissors for suture removal.
To learn single and double hand knots by using the specimen thread given.

topics.title: Bone marrow aspiration
objectives: Review the indications and contraindications of a bone marrow aspiration and biopsy.
Identify the proper site and equipment required to perform a bone marrow aspiration and biopsy.
Acquire the necessary skills to perform a bone marrow aspiration and biopsy.
Know the potential complications of bone marrow aspirations and biopsies.
Name types of samples collected and its laboratory process.

topics.title: Lumbar puncture
objectives: To know the technique of lumbar puncture including aseptic technique, proper positioning and site of puncture.
To know the equipment required for this procedure.
To know the complications of LP.
To know the indication and contraindication of the procedure.
To know how to collect, process to laboratory and analyse the CSF.

topics.title: Paracentesis
objectives: To know the correct technique of paracentesis including aseptic technique, proper positioning and site of puncture.
To know the aseptic technique and objects used in this procedure.
To know the risks and complications of this procedure.
To know the indication and contraindication of paracentesis.
To know how to analyse the fluid.

topics.title: Thoracentesis
objectives: To know the correct technique of the procedure.
To know the equipment required for this procedure.
To know the risks and complications related to this procedure.
To know the indications and contraindications of thoracentesis.
To know how to collect, process and analyse the fluid.

topics.title: Nasogastric tube insertion
objectives: To know the proper technique of NGT insertion.
To know the equipment used in this procedure.
To know the indication and contraindication of the procedure.
To know the care of the NGT.

general_objectives: Obtain a comprehensive history from patients presenting with common surgical complaints.
Perform a systematic physical examination and identify abnormal findings.
Formulate an appropriate list of differential diagnoses.
Propose a basic management plan, including necessary investigations and treatment options.
Demonstrate effective communication skills and apply relevant clinical knowledge.
Conduct a focused literature review on surgical topics.
Exhibit a high standard of professionalism throughout the rotation.

topics.title: General surgery emergencies
objectives: Identify and manage acute abdominal pain: understand the different causes of acute abdominal pain, including inflammatory, obstructive, and vascular etiologies; perform a comprehensive physical examination to elicit signs of acute abdominal pain; utilize appropriate laboratory tests and imaging modalities to diagnose the underlying cause; initiate appropriate management strategies, including fluid resuscitation, pain control, and specific treatment for the underlying condition.

Recognize and treat common surgical emergencies: appendicitis - identify the clinical presentation, diagnostic approach, and management principles; cholecystitis - understand the pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and treatment options; diverticulitis - recognize the clinical features, diagnostic criteria, and treatment strategies; perforated viscus - identify the signs and symptoms and initiate immediate surgical intervention.

Understand the principles of resuscitation and shock management: recognize the signs and symptoms of shock, including hypovolemia, cardiogenic shock, and septic shock; implement appropriate resuscitation strategies, including fluid administration and oxygen supplementation; monitor hemodynamic parameters closely to assess the effectiveness of resuscitation efforts.

Appreciate the importance of perioperative care in preventing complications: identify potential risk factors for surgical complications, such as advanced age, comorbidities, and malnutrition; optimize preoperative patient preparation to minimize perioperative risks; implement appropriate perioperative care measures, including deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis, antibiotic prophylaxis, and glycemic control; provide comprehensive postoperative care to prevent complications and promote recovery.

topics.title: Perioperative care and surgical complications
objectives: Describe the principles of perioperative care: preoperative evaluation - understand the importance of a thorough preoperative assessment to identify potential risks and optimize patient condition; intraoperative management - recognize the key principles of intraoperative care, including anesthesia, surgical technique, and fluid management; postoperative care - implement appropriate postoperative care strategies, including pain management, wound care, and nutritional support.

Identify and manage common surgical complications: infections - recognize the signs and symptoms of surgical site infections and initiate appropriate antibiotic therapy; bleeding - identify the causes and management strategies for postoperative bleeding; wound healing problems - understand the factors that contribute to wound healing problems and implement preventive measures; pulmonary complications - recognize the risk factors and management principles for pulmonary complications, such as pneumonia and atelectasis.

Understand the importance of risk stratification and complication prevention: identify patients at high risk for surgical complications and implement appropriate preventive strategies; utilize risk stratification tools to guide preoperative decision-making and resource allocation; employ evidence-based practices to minimize perioperative complications and improve patient outcomes.

Appreciate the role of the surgeon in coordinating perioperative care: recognize the surgeon's responsibility for leading and coordinating perioperative care; effectively communicate with other healthcare providers to ensure a comprehensive and patient-centered approach to care; advocate for patient safety and quality improvement initiatives in perioperative care.

topics.title: Postoperative fever / respiratory distress / chest pain / hypotension
objectives: Knowledge: The causes of postoperative fever.
Knowledge: The causes of respiratory symptoms (pulmonary collapse/pneumonia and pulmonary embolism), investigations and principles of management.
Knowledge: The causes of chest pain in the postoperative period.
Knowledge: The causes of hypotension (postoperative bleeding).
Knowledge: The approach to a patient with fever, respiratory symptoms, chest pain and hypotension.
Knowledge: Principles of management.

History taking: Details of the pain (location, severity, radiation, relation to breathing, shortness of breath); details of associated symptoms in patients with fever to suggest its cause; obtain history of co-morbid conditions (previous MI, hypertension, smoking).

Examination: Vital signs; pulse oximetry; examination of respiratory system; examination of cardiovascular system; examination of limb for DVT/thrombophlebitis; examination of abdomen for distension and tenderness for abdominal cause of fever (intra-abdominal collection/abscess/anastomotic leak); examination of the wound for infection; examine the neck wound in patients who have undergone thyroidectomy (respiratory distress, tense neck wound and wound hematoma); examine the nasogastric tube aspirate, abdominal drain, neck drains for patients with post-operative hypotension due to bleeding.

Investigation: Formulate a rational investigation plan and interpret the results of: complete blood count (leukocytosis, hemoglobin); biochemistry (ABG, troponin, electrolytes); ECG; chest x-ray (effusion, pneumonia); Doppler study of the venous system of lower extremities; CT angiogram of chest and lower extremities; collection of blood/urine/pus for culture (both aerobic and anaerobic).

Treatment: General measures (oxygen, analgesia); resuscitation with IV fluids and blood products; antibiotics/chest physiotherapy/oxygen for respiratory complications; drainage/exploration for intra-abdominal collection and leak; cardiology consultation for acute MI; anticoagulation for pulmonary embolism.

Communication: Explain to the patient and his relatives the problem, provisional diagnosis and management plan with the help of a senior; observe the process of communication with cardiologist, intensivists, etc.
Attitude: Show empathy while communicating.

topics.title: Abdominal wall / hernia
objectives: Knowledge: Discuss the components of a hernia (defect, sac, neck, fundus, contents).
Knowledge: Discuss the basic clinical features of all hernias (reduce on lying down or with direct pressure and have expansile cough impulse).
Knowledge: Discuss the different types of common abdominal wall hernias, their presentation and complications.
Knowledge: Recognize divarication of the rectus muscle.
Knowledge: Discuss the differential diagnosis of swellings in the groin.
Knowledge: Discuss the principles of operative management of hernias.
Knowledge: Recognize unusual abdominal wall hernias (Spigelian, obturator, gluteal and lumbar).
Knowledge: Recognize swellings in the abdominal wall other than hernias (hematoma of rectus sheath, desmoid tumor).

History: Elicit a comprehensive history of abdominal wall swelling including: duration, location and size of the swelling; associated complications (pain, irreducibility, bowel obstruction, systemic symptoms); previous abdominal surgeries (incisional hernia, direct inguinal hernia) and post-operative complications (wound infection, lung infection, cough); occupation (heavy work, lifting heavy objects); rise in abdominal pressure (lower urinary tract outflow obstruction: stricture in a young male, prostate in elderly male, prolapse of bladder in female; chronic cough - chronic bronchitis; constipation; ascites; intra-abdominal masses; pregnancy); multiple pregnancies.

Examination: General exam & systemic exam; local examination - appreciate the importance of examining the patient both lying down and standing; demonstrate how to differentiate intra-abdominal swellings from swellings in the abdominal wall; differentiate inguinoscrotal swellings from scrotal swellings (it is possible to get above the swelling in scrotal swellings); differentiate inguinal from femoral hernia; demonstrate the position, size, shape, composition, reducibility, tenderness of abdominal wall swellings.
Differential diagnosis: Propose differential diagnosis of groin swellings; propose differential diagnosis of inguinoscrotal swellings; propose differential diagnosis of abdominal wall swellings.
Investigations: Choose appropriate investigations for the patients; appreciate the role and importance of imaging (US, CT, MRI) in the assessment of patients with abdominal wall pathology.

Management: Know the principles of surgical repair of hernias; be familiar with the synthetic meshes that are used; know the complications of surgery and their management; know the preventive measures to reduce infective complications (avoid surgery in presence of systemic infection, shaving the patient in the operating theater, prophylactic antibiotic, avoid contamination of the mesh); observe the process of consent taking for interventional procedures and/or surgery.
Communication skills: Explain to the patient and his/her relatives the problem, provisional diagnosis and management plan with the help of a senior.

Attitude: Show a commitment to the patient right from the process of history taking till discharge; follow the patient's investigations; monitor the patient's progress; observe or participate in the surgery being performed.

topics.title: Neck swellings
objectives: Knowledge: Have a sound knowledge of thyroid swellings; common swellings in the midline and lateral neck; common neck swellings in children, adults and elderly patients; causes of cervical lymphadenopathy; the principles of management of common neck swellings.

History: Elicit a detailed relevant history of the swelling, its duration, associated pain and relation to eating (a long history is generally associated with benign, while a short history is mostly linked to malignant, and inflammatory swellings are generally painful; swellings that appear while eating are mostly from salivary glands).

History: The commonest swelling in the neck is an enlarged lymph node commonly due to infection or secondary deposits; a history of systemic illness (malaise, fever, rigors, contact) may indicate infective cause; elicit a history of contact with a patient with tuberculosis; take a history of smoking and chronic alcohol consumption if malignancy is suspected (risk factors for aero-digestive malignancy).
History: A history of enlargement of nodes in other areas would indicate generalized lymphadenopathy (infective or lympho-proliferative conditions).
History: Elicit history of pain or ulcers in the mouth, dental caries, ENT symptoms, change of voice, ulcers or swellings over the head and face.
History: Dysphagia is associated with esophageal malignancy, pharyngeal pouch, thyroid with retrosternal extension.
History: Breast, respiratory and GI symptoms should be elicited if the swelling is in the lower lateral neck; also elicit history of neuro-vascular symptoms of the upper limb (cervical rib).
History: Propose a differential diagnosis based on the age, presentation and location of the swelling.

Physical examination: General - look for generalized lymphadenopathy, weight loss & pallor. Examination of the neck - describe the swelling and note its location, size, shape, surface, etc. Inspection - situation (branchial cyst along the anterior border of sternomastoid at the junction of upper and middle third; branchial fistula at the junction of lower and middle third; cystic hygroma in the posterior triangle; Virchow's node, cervical rib and aneurysm of subclavian artery in the posterior triangle; aneurysm along the line of carotid vessels; carotid body tumor at the upper level of thyroid cartilage); midline swellings from above downwards (submental lymph node, sublingual dermoid, lipoma, subhyoid bursa, thyroglossal cyst, thyroid, lymph node in suprasternal space, retrosternal goiter, dermoid); an enlarged parotid salivary gland usually elevates the ear lobe (examine the facial nerve and carry out intra-oral examination for deeper lobe enlargement); swellings that move on deglutition (thyroglossal cyst, subhyoid bursa, thyroid gland and nodes attached to larynx and trachea); skin - ulcers, scars (tuberculosis); sinuses (tuberculosis, osteomyelitis of jaw, actinomycosis, thyroglossal fistula or branchial fistula); describe skin changes (redness, edema & dilated veins). Palpation - best palpated from behind with neck flexed slightly and turned to the side; carotid body tumor and aneurysm move transversely; determine relation to sternomastoid; pulsatile swellings; submandibular triangle swellings; systematic lymph node examination (enlarged fleshy nodes suggest lymphoma; matted liquefied nodes adherent to skin suggest tuberculosis; painless, firm to hard, fixed nodes suggest metastases); examine the draining area if the lymph node is suspicious (remove dentures and palpate the oral cavity for induration; if Virchow's node is enlarged examine the arm, breast, chest and abdomen including the testis). Auscultation - a bruit may be heard in aneurysm or carotid body tumor. Examination of the upper limb in case of cervical rib - neurovascular exam, Adson's test.

Physical examination: After the examination, be able to answer: are there more than one swelling (lymph nodes)? Where is the swelling? Is the swelling solid or cystic (solid: lymph nodes, carotid body tumor; cystic: cystic hygroma, cold abscess, branchial cyst, pharyngeal pouch)? Does it move with deglutition (thyroglossal cyst, thyroid gland)?

Differential diagnosis: After analyzing history and physical examination, arrive at an anatomical and pathological diagnosis of the neck swelling; if the swelling is an enlarged lymph node, probable causes are: infection (non-specific tonsillitis, brucellosis, tuberculosis, glandular fever, toxoplasmosis, cat scratch fever, syphilis); metastatic tumor from head, neck, chest and abdomen; lympho-proliferative (lymphoma, lymphosarcoma); sarcoidosis.

Investigations: Formulate an appropriate investigation plan to arrive at or confirm the diagnosis - blood (CBC, ESR, CRP, LDH, brucella titres, Paul Bunnell test, Kveim test, etc.); tuberculin test; thorough ENT examination including direct laryngoscopy; pan endoscopy (direct laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy and esophagoscopy with blind biopsies in case of unknown primary); radiology; ultrasound, ultrasound-guided biopsy, aspiration; CT scan of head & neck (chest and abdomen if necessary); fine needle biopsy; excisional biopsy.

Management: Formulate a plan and know the principles of management for: thyroid swelling; lymphadenopathy; salivary gland swellings; thyroglossal cyst; carotid artery aneurysm; carotid body tumor; cystic hygroma; branchial cyst and fistula; cervical rib.
Basic procedural skills: Observe indirect and direct laryngoscopy; observe needle biopsy; suture removal.

Communication skills: Explain to the patient and his relatives the provisional diagnosis and management plan with the help of a senior; observe the process of consent taking for interventional procedures and/or surgery.

topics.title: Thyroid swelling
objectives: Knowledge: Recognize and examine a thyroid swelling.

Knowledge: List causes of solitary thyroid swelling (dominant nodule in a multinodular goiter; thyroid cyst; hemorrhage into a nodule; adenoma, could be toxic; carcinoma - papillary, follicular or medullary; thyroiditis restricted to one lobe).

Knowledge: List the causes of generalized thyromegaly (diffuse/physiological goiter; multinodular goiter; thyroiditis - Hashimoto's, Riedel's, De Quervain's; malignancy - anaplastic, medullary, lymphoma).
Knowledge: Discuss the principles of management of types of thyroid swellings.
Knowledge: Interpret thyroid function tests.
Knowledge: Complications of thyroid operations.
Knowledge: Discuss the features of hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism (understand the difference between hyperthyroidism and thyrotoxicosis).

History taking: Details of the swelling, duration, onset, progress, pain; history of exposure to radiation (occupational, accidental or as therapy); local pressure symptoms, dyspnea, change in voice, discomfort during swallowing (would indicate malignant change or more commonly retrosternal extension); symptoms pertaining to eyes (prominence, diplopia, redness as seen in Graves' disease); symptoms to suggest thyroid dysfunction (hypothyroidism: increase in weight, slow thought, speech and action, intolerance to cold, loss of hair, fatigue, constipation; hyperthyroidism: irritability, insomnia, palpitations, increase in appetite but loss of weight, wasting, weakness, preference for cold weather, excessive sweating, amenorrhea); family history of thyroid disease (endemic, dyshormonogenesis, MEN syndrome); family history of abdominal surgery (pheochromocytoma, FAP are associated with thyroid malignancy); does the patient come from an endemic area (>7% prevalence for thyroid disease); history of medications (anti-tubercular drugs like PAS, rifampicin, phenytoin, amiodarone, lithium).

Physical examination (general): Observe the whole patient - is the patient restless, nervous and fidgety or slow and lethargic? Under clothed or over clothed? Thin or fat? (proximal girdle wasting is seen with thyrotoxicosis); pulse (tachycardia and arrhythmias with thyrotoxicosis, bradycardia with hypothyroid state); sweaty hands suggest hyperthyroid state; look for fine, fast finger tremors; look for skin changes over the tibia (pre-tibial myxedema); look at the fingers for thyrotoxic acropachy; examine the eyes for prominence (differentiate lid retraction from exophthalmos), ophthalmoplegia (diplopia), chemosis, corneal ulceration, lid lag, absence of convergence, absence of forehead wrinkling on looking upwards.

Physical examination (neck): Inspection - is it a thyroid swelling (moves with deglutition)? Is the lower border seen (rules out retrosternal extension)? Is it localized or generalized? Note size, situation, surface; note skin changes (prominent veins, pulsation suggest increased vascularity); note the position of the larynx and trachea; inspect for prominent veins (retrosternal extension). Palpation - palpate from behind using long fingers with counter-pressure; ascertain the swelling moves with deglutition and feel for the lower limit; palpate the gland for enlargement, nodules, size, surface, consistency, intrinsic thyroid mobility & deviation of larynx and trachea; look for thrills; palpate for carotid pulsations behind and above the lobe (don't palpate both carotid vessels simultaneously); palpate for enlarged lymph nodes. Percussion - percuss over the sternum (dullness suggests retrosternal extension or enlarged mediastinal nodes). Auscultation - over the thyroid gland for bruits as seen in Graves' disease.

Physical examination: At the end of the examination, be able to answer: Is it a thyroid swelling? Is the patient euthyroid, hypo- or hyperthyroid? Is it localized or generalized thyromegaly? Does it extend retrosternally? What is the probable diagnosis?

Investigation: Formulate an investigation plan for patients with thyroid swelling, rationalize the investigations ordered, and interpret the results of: thyroid function tests; autoimmune tests for thyroid disorders; tumor markers (thyroglobulin, calcitonin); ultrasound of thyroid; nuclear scan (thyroid scan & whole-body scan); fine needle aspiration cytology; CT scan of the neck.

Treatment: Know the principles of treatment of hyperthyroidism (anti-thyroid drugs, radioiodine ablation, surgery); treatment and monitoring of patients with hypothyroid state; the principles of various surgical options and their indications (hemi-thyroidectomy, sub-total thyroidectomy, complete/total thyroidectomy, near-total thyroidectomy).

Thyroglossal cyst and ectopic thyroid: Make a diagnosis of thyroglossal cyst (midline cystic swelling, moves with deglutition and on protruding the tongue); be familiar with the rare possibility of ectopic thyroid (sublingual, subhyoid in the midline); know the complications of thyroglossal cysts (infection, abscess, fistula) and its investigations (ultrasound, nuclear scan).

Communication: Explain to the patient and his relatives the problem, provisional diagnosis and management plan with the help of a senior; observe the process of consent taking for interventional procedures and/or surgery.
Attitude: Show empathy while communicating.

topics.title: Informed consent and ethical considerations in surgery
objectives: Understand the principles of informed consent in surgical practice.

Describe the key elements of informed consent, including: disclosure of material risks and benefits of the procedure; discussion of alternative treatment options; opportunity to ask questions and clarify concerns; voluntary decision-making.

Recognize ethical considerations in surgical decision-making, such as: autonomy - respecting patient autonomy and self-determination; beneficence - acting in the patient's best interest and promoting their well-being; non-maleficence - avoiding harm and minimizing potential risks; justice - ensuring fair and equitable access to surgical care.
Discuss the role of informed consent and ethical considerations in preventing patient harm and promoting positive surgical outcomes.
Discuss several ethical cases in general surgeries.

topics.title: Burns
objectives: Understand the classification and pathophysiology of burns, including: degree of burn (first-degree, second-degree, third-degree, and fourth-degree burns); burn mechanisms (thermal burns, chemical burns, electrical burns, and radiation burns).

Recognize the clinical presentation and management of burn injuries, including: assessment of burn depth and extent; fluid resuscitation and electrolyte balance; wound care and infection control; pain management; nutritional support.
Discuss the principles of burn prevention and public health strategies to reduce burn incidence.

topics.title: Ulcers and wound healing
objectives: Knowledge: The difference between a wound and an ulcer.
Knowledge: Common ulcers in surgical practice.
Knowledge: Phases of wound healing (inflammatory, proliferative & remodeling).
Knowledge: Types of wound healing (primary, secondary & tertiary).
Knowledge: Systemic and local factors that promote healing.
Knowledge: Systemic and local factors that hinder healing.
Knowledge: Complications of wound healing.
Knowledge: Technique of taking a swab for culture.

History taking: Details of the ulcer, duration, onset, progress, pain; history of diabetes mellitus, injury, ischemia, peripheral neuropathy, radiation & immune compromised state; drug history (steroids, immunosuppressants, smoking); systemic inflammatory response syndrome.
General examination: Observe the whole patient paying attention to nutritional status; bed bound, bony prominences; look for skin changes of vitamin deficiencies; vital signs.

Local examination: Able to differentiate a benign from malignant ulcer; describe the features of common benign ulcers - varicose/diabetic/trophic; principles of management of malignant ulcer (basal cell/squamous cell) and malignant melanoma.

Investigation: Formulate a rational investigation plan for patients with ulcer and interpret the results of: complete blood count (leukocytosis, hemoglobin, megaloblasts: vitamin B-12 deficiency); biochemistry (serum proteins, blood sugar, lipid profile, HbA1c); swab for culture; x-ray for evidence of osteomyelitis; Doppler study of the peripheral vessels in case of lower extremity ulcers; CT angiogram.

Treatment: General supportive measures (correction of anemia, nutritional state, trace elements); wound dressings (management of pain, discharge, infection & edema); introduction to Vacuum Assisted Closure (VAC) dressings.

Communication: Explain to the patient and his relatives the problem, provisional diagnosis and management plan with the help of a senior; observe the process of consent taking for interventional procedures and/or surgery.
Attitude: Show empathy while communicating.

topics.title: Shock & trauma
objectives: Understand the definition, pathophysiology, and classification of shock, including: hypovolemic shock (caused by fluid loss, such as from hemorrhage or severe dehydration); cardiogenic shock (caused by impaired heart function); obstructive shock (caused by obstruction of blood flow, such as from a pulmonary embolism or cardiac tamponade).
Recognize the signs and symptoms of shock, including: hypotension; tachycardia; tachypnea; cool, clammy skin; altered mental status.

Describe the principles of resuscitation and shock management, including: airway management and oxygenation; fluid resuscitation to restore blood volume; vasopressor therapy to maintain blood pressure; treatment of underlying causes.
Discuss the principles of trauma management, including: initial assessment and stabilization; identification and treatment of injuries; damage control surgery; critical care management.

topics.title: Pediatric surgery emergencies
objectives: Knowledge: Explain the anatomical and physiological differences in children that impact the presentation and management of surgical emergencies.
Knowledge: Discuss the developmental and psychological considerations relevant to acute surgical conditions in pediatric patients.

Knowledge: Identify the clinical features, underlying pathophysiology and potential complications of: acute appendicitis; hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; intussusception; intestinal malrotation and midgut volvulus; scrotal swellings (incarcerated inguinal hernia and testicular torsion).
Knowledge: Outline the approach to diagnosis and initial management of acute pediatric surgical emergencies.
Knowledge: Emphasize the importance of early recognition, prompt stabilization, and timely surgical referral.
Knowledge: Describe the principles of family-centered care and the role of interprofessional teamwork in pediatric emergency management.

History taking: Obtain a focused history, including: onset, progression, and nature of presenting symptoms (e.g., abdominal pain, vomiting, scrotal pain or swelling); associated symptoms such as fever, lethargy, or irritability; feeding habits, bowel and urinary patterns, and recent infections or trauma; relevant past medical, surgical, and family history.

Clinical examination: Perform a general and focused physical examination tailored to pediatric patients; assess hydration status, vital signs, and overall clinical stability; perform an abdominal and genitourinary examination to identify signs of surgical pathology (e.g., guarding, rebound tenderness, irreducible hernia, high-riding testis).

Differential diagnosis: Generate appropriate differential diagnoses for: acute abdomen in neonates, infants and children; non-bilious and bilious vomiting; groin and scrotal swellings (including testicular torsion, hydrocele, inguinal hernia); causes of acute scrotal pain.

Investigations: Select and interpret appropriate initial investigations (e.g., CBC, CRP, electrolytes, urinalysis); recognize indications for imaging studies including abdominal ultrasound, Doppler ultrasound and plain abdominal radiographs; select and interpret appropriate imaging studies for each condition and recognize key diagnostic signs; understand the limitations and benefits of each modality in pediatric patients.

Management: Describe initial steps in stabilization of a child with a surgical emergency (e.g., fluid resuscitation, analgesia); outline the general principles of preoperative and postoperative care in children; outline the indications, timing, and general approach to surgical management for each acute pediatric surgical condition; observe or participate in surgical procedures, when possible, under supervision.

Communication skills: Demonstrate effective and empathetic communication with pediatric patients and their caregivers; explain diagnoses and management plans in clear, non-technical language; participate in shared decision-making and respect family concerns and values.

topics.title: Abdominal pain
objectives: Knowledge: Know the definition of acute abdomen.
Knowledge: Be able to differentiate between acute and chronic abdominal pain.
Knowledge: Know the common causes of acute abdomen.
Knowledge: Know that extra-abdominal diseases can present as acute abdomen.
Knowledge: Be familiar with acute abdominal conditions that need immediate surgery.

History taking: Elicit a full history of pain (nature, duration, onset, location, aggravating & relieving factors, progression); elicit associated symptoms (appetite, nausea, vomiting, bowel movements, abdominal distension, fever, jaundice & hematuria); elicit medication history & past history of surgery; elicit gynecological history and history of travel abroad; formulate a differential diagnosis.

Physical examination: General physical examination - identify pallor, dehydration, weight loss, lymphadenopathy and jaundice; recognize the features of septic shock (hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnoea and fever); systematically examine the abdomen (obtain verbal consent and be sensitive to the patient). Inspection - is the abdomen distended (localized or generalized)? Umbilicus (everted, stretched, displaced, hernia, nodule); scars; distended veins (differentiate IVC & portal vein obstruction); visible peristalsis (gastric, intestinal); bruises (Grey Turner's sign, Cullen's sign); examine hernial orifices. Palpation - demonstrate superficial and deep palpation; elicit tenderness, guarding and rigidity (Murphy's sign, Rovsing's sign, psoas sign, cough tenderness, heel tap); detect organomegaly/mass and describe its physical characteristics. Percussion - identify tympanic note over the hepatic area seen in perforated viscus; demonstrate shifting dullness. Auscultation - identify normal and abnormal bowel sounds; appreciate other sounds (bruit, rubs).

Physical examination (special circumstances): Examination of the abdomen of a pregnant patient (viscera are pushed up; guarding is difficult to elicit); children (examine in the presence of or with the help of parents; use the child's own hand to palpate; be gentle and sensitive); acute abdomen in the immune-compromised & elderly patients (signs are unreliable; guarding may be masked or minimal); perform a rectal examination under supervision.
Differential diagnosis: Formulate a differential diagnosis based on the symptoms and signs in order of their strength.

Investigations: List the required investigations and their use; consider other investigations that would be necessary to assess patient's fitness for surgery; learn to read a plain x-ray of the abdomen and recognize free air in the peritoneal cavity, ground glass appearance, mass effect & intestinal obstruction; be familiar with: ultrasound; CT scan (MDCT, CECT, plain CT); virtual colonoscopy; MRI; endoscopy (upper & lower GI, including ERCP); needle biopsy.
Management: Formulate a management plan for the various conditions; when to admit? Analgesia? Observation? Emergency surgery, etc.

Communication: Explain to the patient and his relatives the problem, provisional diagnosis and management plan with the help of a senior; observe the process of consent taking for interventional procedures and/or surgery.
Attitude: Show empathy while communicating; be sensitive to patients with regards to pain and privacy.

topics.title: Upper GI bleeding
objectives: Knowledge: Define upper GI bleeding, massive GI bleeding and obscure GI bleeding.
Knowledge: Discuss the clinical presentation of patients with upper GI bleeding.
Knowledge: Discuss the significance of changes in the color of blood in the stools (melena, maroon & hematochezia).
Knowledge: List common causes of upper GI bleeding (acid peptic ulcer, acute gastritis: stress, NSAID; esophageal varices, Mallory-Weiss tear, gastric cancer).
Knowledge: Discuss the principles of initial evaluation and management of upper GI bleeding.
Knowledge: Discuss the principles of management of common causative disorders of upper GI bleeding (duodenal ulcer, gastritis, portal hypertension, gastric cancer).

History taking: Amount, color of the vomitus; associated symptoms (weakness, dizziness and syncope); color of stools (melena is usually due to upper GI bleed but can be seen with lower GI bleed as well - right sided colonic pathology; sometimes a brisk upper GI bleed presents with bright red stools); dyspepsia, previous acid peptic disorder, upper GI endoscopy, medications (proton pump inhibitor, H. pylori treatment, NSAID, aspirin); vomiting or severe retching; chronic alcohol abuse; hepatitis or pancreatitis (cause portal hypertension).

Physical examination: Do a general examination of a patient with GI bleed (general status, pallor, jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy); assess vital signs (temperature, blood pressure, respiratory rate, pulse rate, rhythm, character, volume); carry out a general physical examination (lymphadenopathy, cardiovascular, respiratory); conduct a focused complete abdominal and rectal exam.
Differential diagnosis: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient with blood in the stool (be sure to include benign, malignant and inflammatory causes).

Investigations: Explain the significance of doing hematological tests of CBC and coagulation profile, blood cross match; liver function tests, urea and electrolytes; explain significance of doing a gastroscopy and colonoscopy; discuss the order of the radiological diagnostic workup for GI bleed (RBC nuclear tagged study, CT angio and conventional angiography).

Management: Discuss the steps of managing a patient with acute upper GI bleed; discuss the interventional and surgical treatment options for patients with acute GI bleed; discuss the complications associated with hemorrhagic shock.
Prevention: Discuss the role of diet, medication, alcohol, caffeine, and H. pylori treatment in the natural history and prevention of GI hemorrhage.
Attitude: Show empathy and professionalism while communicating and examining a patient with GI bleed.

topics.title: Lower GI bleeding
objectives: Knowledge: Define lower GI bleeding, massive GI bleeding and obscure GI bleeding.
Knowledge: Discuss the significance of changes in the color of blood (hematochezia, melena, maroon).
Knowledge: List the common causes of rectal bleeding.
Knowledge: Discuss the principles of initial management of rectal bleeding.
Knowledge: Describe how to identify patients who need admission.
Knowledge: Discuss the principles of management of common causative disorders of rectal bleeding (diverticulitis, angiodysplasia, colonic polyps, malignancy, colitis, hemorrhoids and rectal ulcer).

History taking: The duration of bleeding, amount, association with defecation, pain, presence of mucus, constitutional symptoms (fever, light headedness, weakness), abdominal cramps; blood-streaked stools, perianal pain, blood on the toilet paper/toilet bowl may be associated with perianal pathology (fissure in ano, hemorrhoids); altered bowel habits might suggest possibility of malignancy; constipation is common with diverticular disease and hemorrhoids; history of peptic ulcer disease, liver disease, cirrhosis, inflammatory bowel disease, coagulopathy, and radiation; drugs (NSAIDs, aspirin, warfarin); color of stools (bright red stools suggest left sided bleeding, maroon stools suggest right sided bleeding, melena indicates upper GI bleeding, however this is not entirely accurate).

Physical examination: Do a general examination of a patient with GI bleed (general status, pallor, jaundice, lymphadenopathy); assess vital signs; determine the severity of bleeding; conduct a focused complete abdominal and rectal exam.

Differential diagnosis: Develop a differential diagnosis list considering the history and the age of the patient: colonic diverticula; angiodysplasia; colonic neoplasms (polyps and malignancy); inflammatory bowel disease; colitis (infectious, ischemic, radiation).

Investigations: Propose and discuss the order of the diagnostic workup for GI bleed, depending on rate of bleeding and hemodynamic status of the patient (endoscopy, radionuclide scan and angiography); explain the significance of CBC, coagulation profile and blood cross match; explain the significance of doing a gastroscopy (10% of patients have bleeding from upper GI source) and colonoscopy; propose specific tests for Meckel's diverticulum.

Management: Insert NG tube - a clear bile-stained aspirate generally excludes bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz; discuss the steps of managing a patient with acute lower GI bleed (resuscitation & initial assessment, localization of bleeding, intervention to stop bleeding); discuss the interventional and surgical treatment options and their complications: endoscopy (bipolar probe coagulation, injection of vasoconstrictors, sclerosants, metallic clips, argon coagulation); angiography (selective injection of vasopressin, embolization using microcoils, gelfoam); emergency surgery (indications: hemodynamic instability, persistent or recurrent bleeding, transfusion of more than 4 units of PRBC); discuss the complications associated with hemorrhagic shock; discuss the diagnosis and treatment of colo-rectal cancer and colonic polyps; discuss how to manage the different types of hemorrhoids; propose a management plan for chronic GI bleed (patients presenting with iron deficiency anemia).

Communication: Elicit history of high-risk behavior, such as smoking, alcohol consumption; obtain informed consent for chosen line of management; propose a plan to break bad news to a patient with a malignant condition.
Attitude: Show empathy and professionalism while communicating and examining a patient with GI bleed.

topics.title: Abdominal distension / bowel obstruction
objectives: Knowledge: Differentiate between acute and chronic abdominal distention.
Knowledge: Outline features of acute intestinal obstruction.
Knowledge: Differentiate between small and large gut obstruction.
Knowledge: Be able to recognize mechanical obstruction and paralytic ileus.
Knowledge: List the causes of small gut obstruction.
Knowledge: List the causes of large gut obstruction.
Knowledge: List the causes of paralytic ileus.
Knowledge: List the causes of chronic abdominal distension (ascites, tuberculosis, ovarian cyst).
Knowledge: Discuss the water and electrolyte imbalance that occurs with intestinal obstruction.
Knowledge: Discuss the principles of management of intestinal obstruction.
Knowledge: Read plain x-ray of the abdomen and recognize: intestinal obstruction; paralytic ileus; free air in the peritoneal cavity; air within the bowel wall.
Knowledge: Identify abdominal mass.

History taking: Obtain and document a detailed history and determine: if the patient has intestinal obstruction or abdominal distention; the probable level of obstruction and differentiate between small and large gut obstruction (upper small bowel, lower small bowel, large bowel); the probable cause of obstruction (previous history of acute abdomen, surgery, hernia, history to suggest diverticulitis, colonic malignancy).

Physical examination: Recognize the features of dehydration; identify the features of septic shock (hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnoea and fever); systematically examine the abdomen - inspection (distension whether central or generalized; umbilicus - everted, stretched, caput medusa; scars; hernial orifices - umbilical, inguinal and femoral; distended veins - differentiate IVC & portal vein obstruction; visible peristalsis - differentiate pyloric, small and large gut obstruction); palpation (identify guarding and rigidity; elicit tenderness; detect organomegaly; abdominal mass); percussion (demonstrate shifting dullness; identify liver span); auscultation (recognize exaggerated bowel sounds; identify absent sounds).

Management: Propose a differential diagnosis; formulate the management plan including the investigations; interpret the results of CBC (leukocytosis), urea and electrolytes (recognize the effect of dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities due to vomiting) and ascitic fluid analysis (differentiate between transudate and exudates); x-ray abdomen, ultrasound and CT; lower GI endoscopy.

Basic procedural skills: Perform rectal examination under supervision; insert a nasogastric tube under supervision; observe insertion of a central line including reading of central venous pressure and chest x-ray; insertion of Foley catheter.

Communication skills: Explain to the patient and his relatives the problem, provisional diagnosis and management plan with the help of a senior; observe the process of consent taking for interventional procedures and/or surgery.

Attitude: Show a commitment to the patient right from the process of history taking till the discharge; follow up the patient's investigations; monitor the patient's progress; observe or assist the surgery being performed.

topics.title: Abdominal mass
objectives: Knowledge: Systematically prepare and examine the abdomen.
Knowledge: Systematically describe the physical characteristics of an abdominal mass (location, size, surface, borders, mobility, movement with respiration).
Knowledge: Differentiate abdominal mass from abdominal distention.
Knowledge: Differentiate between abdominal wall swellings from intra-abdominal masses.
Knowledge: Differentiate intra-abdominal mass from retroperitoneal mass.
Knowledge: Recognize retroperitoneal masses.
Knowledge: Differentiate hepatomegaly from right kidney.
Knowledge: Recognize gall bladder enlargement.
Knowledge: Differentiate splenomegaly from left kidney.
Knowledge: Differentiate pulsatile swellings from swellings that transmit pulsation.
Knowledge: Recognize swellings arising from the pelvis.
Knowledge: Formulate a differential diagnosis based on the physical characteristics and the anatomical location of the mass.
Knowledge: Outline the relevant investigations.
Knowledge: Learn to read CT scan of the abdomen.

History taking: Take a detailed history pertaining to the mass including associated symptoms like pain, vomiting, appetite, weight loss, bowel habits and constitutional symptoms; also include social history, family history, menstrual history (if applicable); after obtaining a detailed history come to a reasonable conclusion as to the anatomical origin/pathology of the mass.

Physical examination (general): Recognize jaundice, anemia, malnutrition (cachexia), and edema; look for Virchow's lymph node; look for superficial thrombophlebitis (may be associated with visceral malignancy).

Physical examination (abdominal): Inspection - is the mass seen, where is it located, does it move with respiration? Umbilicus - presence of Sister Joseph nodules; distended veins (differentiate IVC & portal vein obstruction). Palpation - elicit tenderness; recognize guarding and rigidity; identify the mass and appreciate its physical characteristics (location, size, surface, borders, does it cross the midline, mobility, movement with respiration); detect organomegaly. Percussion - establish the percussion note over the mass; demonstrate shifting dullness; identify liver span; demonstrate succussion splash. Auscultation - appreciate abnormal sounds, bruit, rubs (hepatic, splenic); note the nature of bowel sounds. Perform digital examination under supervision; look for pelvic deposits (Blumer's shelf). Recognize retroperitoneal mass (usually fixed, resonant, but if they reach abdominal wall would be dull, move little with respiration, transmit aortic pulsation).

Differential diagnosis and investigations: List the probable differential diagnosis; outline the management plan including the investigations; list the relevant investigations; interpret the results of CBC, urea and electrolytes, ascitic fluid analysis; learn to read plain x-rays of abdomen, ultrasound and CT; observe US/CT guided biopsy; observe lower and upper GI endoscopy.
Basic procedural skills: Perform rectal examination under supervision; insert nasogastric tube under supervision.

Communication skills: Explain to the patient and his relatives the problem, provisional diagnosis and management plan with the help of a senior; observe the process of consent taking for interventional procedures/surgery.

topics.title: Jaundice
objectives: Knowledge: List the causes of jaundice and in particular the common causes of extra-hepatic biliary obstruction (e.g. gallstones, carcinoma of pancreas, chronic pancreatitis, bile duct stricture).
Knowledge: Describe how to investigate a patient with jaundice.

Knowledge: Describe the principles of management of jaundice secondary to CBD obstruction including preoperative preparation of patients with obstructive jaundice (in particular, gallstone cholangitis, carcinoma of head of pancreas, chronic pancreatitis).

Knowledge: Understand the classification and pathogenesis of jaundice - pre-hepatic jaundice (sickle cell disease, thalassemia, hereditary spherocytosis, hypersplenism); hepatic jaundice (hepatitis, cirrhosis, drug induced, autoimmune, infiltrative); post-hepatic jaundice (gallstone, cholangiocarcinoma, peri-ampullary carcinoma, carcinoma of pancreas, bile duct strictures, chronic pancreatitis, choledochal cyst).
Knowledge: Discuss the pathophysiology of obstructive jaundice.
Knowledge: Discuss the common causes and complications of jaundice.
Knowledge: Diagnose and investigate a patient with jaundice.
Knowledge: How to differentiate the various types of jaundice based on investigations, LFT, urine analysis (pre-hepatic, hepatic and post-hepatic).
Knowledge: Discuss the principles of surgical management of obstructive jaundice.
Knowledge: Courvoisier's law.

History taking: Elicit a detailed history that would establish the type and cause of jaundice (mild in case of pre-hepatic, severe in hepatic and post-hepatic) and associated complications like coagulopathy, renal failure, and hepatic encephalopathy. This would include: jaundice and abdominal pain (onset, duration, severity and progress - sudden, short duration, severe with colicky right hypochondriac pain is suggestive of choledocholithiasis; steady increase over weeks with backache is suggestive of carcinoma of head of pancreas; dull right hypochondriac ache with mild to moderate jaundice over days to weeks is suggestive of infectious hepatitis); urine discoloration, discoloration of stools, pruritus, weight loss, fever, bleeding tendency and altered sensorium; history of biliary surgery; alcohol abuse; family history of hemoglobinopathy; drug abuse, travel abroad, exposure to blood products, sexual history; drugs (paracetamol, erythromycin, halothane).

Physical examination: General examination - recognize severity of jaundice, scratch marks, mental status, hepatic tremors, Virchow's node, superficial thrombophlebitis, spider nevi, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, Dupuytren's contracture. Abdominal examination - recognize and demonstrate hepatomegaly, enlarged gallbladder, splenomegaly and ascites.

Differential diagnosis: Arrive at a differential diagnosis based on history, physical examination and investigations, and prioritize them. The common causes are choledocholithiasis, bilio-pancreatic malignancy, infectious hepatitis and hemoglobinopathy.

Investigations: Formulate a rational plan of investigation to arrive at a diagnosis; interpret liver function tests & urine analysis to differentiate pre-hepatic, hepatic or post-hepatic jaundice; interpret full blood count, sickle cell and coagulation screen; name other investigations necessary to assess patient's fitness for surgery; describe the principles and limitations of radiological and other invasive techniques used to define the site and nature of obstructive jaundice including: ultrasound; CT scan; MRCP; endoscopy (ERCP, endoscopic US); needle biopsy of liver.

Management: Know the principles of management of obstructive jaundice: correction of fluid and electrolytes; correction of coagulopathy (vitamin K, FFP); prophylactic antibiotics prior to intervention or surgery; minimizing renal failure by hydrating the patient in the peri-operative period; minimizing hepatic failure by early decompression of the biliary tree (PTC, endoscopic stenting); the principles of management of stones in the CBD (endoscopic removal, removal by laparoscopic or open surgery); basic principles of the treatment of cancer of pancreas, overview of Whipple's procedure and the reconstruction, palliation of patients with advanced cancer of pancreas (triple bypass, internal stenting, celiac plexus ablation); basic principles of the management of patients with chronic pancreatitis; the basics of managing a patient with hepatic encephalopathy.
Basic procedural skills: Perform urine dipstick; insert Foley catheter; observe ERCP & liver biopsy.

Communication skills: Explain to the patient and the relatives the problem, provisional diagnosis and management plan with the help of a senior; observe the process of consent taking for interventional procedures and/or surgery.

Attitude: Show a commitment to the patient right from the process of history taking till the discharge; follow up the patient's investigations; monitor the patient's progress; observe or participate in the surgery being performed.

topics.title: Breast disorders
objectives: Learning objectives: Assess all breast complaints using the Triple assessment method.
Learning objectives: List the causes and types of nipple discharge.
Learning objectives: Differentiate between cyclical and non-cyclical true breast pain, and musculoskeletal pain.
Learning objectives: Differentiate between lactation and non-lactation mastitis and other types of breast inflammation.
Learning objectives: Differentiate between physiological breast changes, aberration of normal breast development and involution (ANDI), benign breast disease and breast cancer.
Learning objectives: List the causes of male breast swellings, i.e. gynecomastia (physiological and pathological) and malignancy.
Knowledge: List the causes of breast lumps; relate between causes of breast infection.
Skills: Relate the difference between benign and malignant; list the different causes of gynecomastia.

History taking: Elicit constitutional symptoms, pain, nipple discharge, swellings, associated symptoms, relation to menstrual cycle; differentiate between cyclical and non-cyclical breast mastalgia; previous breast disorders; drug history, oral contraceptive pill and hormone replacement therapy; family history of breast cancer; personal history such as smoking, obesity and alcohol.

Physical examination: Describe breast lumps in terms of numbers, site, size, shape, surface, margins, attachments to overlying and underlying structures and tenderness; assess mobility and fixation of a lump; differentiate between early, locally advanced and metastatic breast cancer; assess the axilla and the neck for lymphadenopathy and the abdomen for hepatomegaly and ascites.

Differential diagnosis: Propose a differential diagnosis based on analysis of the history and physical examination; propose differential diagnosis for male breast swelling; propose differential diagnosis for acute and chronic breast infection.
Investigations: Assess breast disorders using the triple assessment method: history and examination; imaging (breast US, mammogram and MRI); histopathology (FNAC, core biopsy and open biopsy).

Management: Propose a management plan for different types of benign breast disease; propose a management for a patient recently diagnosed with breast cancer, such as staging investigations and early referral to oncologist; understand the role of the oncologist.
Attitude: Show empathy while communicating; verbal consent and chaperone for examination.
Communication skills: Learn about breaking bad news.

topics.title: Acute perianal conditions
objectives: Knowledge: Outline the common causes of acute perianal pain (perianal abscess, acute fissure in ano, prolapsed hemorrhoids, perianal hematoma, pilonidal sinus).
Knowledge: Apply Goodsall's rule.
Knowledge: Appreciate the process of perianal examination.
Knowledge: List the investigations necessary; formulate a diagnostic workup.
Knowledge: Outline the principles of management of acute perianal conditions.

History taking: Systematically elicit history of pain (nature, duration, onset, location, relation to bowel movement, progression); bleeding per rectum (color, quantity, blood-streaked stools); bowel habits (constipation, straining, use of laxatives); history of inflammatory bowel disease; past history of perianal symptoms or surgery.

Physical examination: Verbal consent, privacy, chaperone, prepare and be sensitive to the patient, examination under supervision. Inspection - recognize signs that indicate painful anal conditions (tenderness, induration, skin tags, perianal hematoma); identify an external opening of fistula in ano; identify the prolapsed hemorrhoids and differentiate them from rectal prolapse; apply Goodsall's rule; differentiate between a fistula in ano and a pilonidal sinus. Palpation under supervision (never perform a digital rectal examination in patients with acute pain) - recognize induration suggesting deep-seated infection; recognize the deep-seated fissure within the external skin tag; identify the fibrous tract around the external opening. Digital examination of the anal canal - appreciate the internal opening; recognize deep-seated induration or tenderness. Proctoscopy (performed only if it is possible to do a digital exam).
Diagnosis: Diagnose common perianal conditions (perianal abscess, fistula in ano, anal fissure, perianal hematoma, hemorrhoids and its complications, rectal prolapse, inflammatory bowel disease).

Investigations: Formulate the investigation plan to arrive at a diagnosis; rationalize their use; investigations necessary to assess patient's fitness for surgery; familiarize with: CT scan of the pelvis; MRI; biopsy of lesions suspected to be malignant.

Management: Formulate a management plan for the various conditions including their preparation for surgery and postoperative care: perianal abscess; fistula in ano; anal fissure; perianal hematoma; hemorrhoids and its complications.

topics.title: Benign colon disorder - diverticulitis
objectives: Knowledge: Describe the pathophysiology and risk factors of diverticulitis.
Knowledge: Explain the clinical presentation, including typical symptoms and complications.
Knowledge: Identify key diagnostic tools, including laboratory tests, imaging, and histopathological findings.
Knowledge: Differentiate uncomplicated from complicated diverticulitis (e.g., perforation, abscess, fistula, obstruction).
Knowledge: Outline the principles of medical and surgical management of diverticulitis.

History taking: Obtain a focused history, including symptoms such as abdominal pain, fever, bowel habit changes, and prior episodes; elicit risk factors like diet, lifestyle, and medication use (e.g., NSAIDs, corticosteroids).
Physical examination: Perform a systematic abdominal examination, identifying signs of peritonitis, localized tenderness (typically left lower quadrant), and possible complications.
Differential diagnosis: Differentiate diverticulitis from other causes of acute abdominal pain, including appendicitis, inflammatory bowel disease, colorectal cancer, and ischemic colitis.

Investigations: Interpret laboratory findings (e.g., leukocytosis, elevated CRP); analyze imaging modalities such as CT scan findings of inflammation, abscess, or perforation; recognize histological features of diverticulitis in resected specimens when applicable.

Management: Discuss conservative (antibiotic therapy, bowel rest) vs. interventional management (drainage, surgery); identify indications for urgent surgical intervention; recognize the role of lifestyle modifications and prevention strategies.

Communication: Effectively explain the diagnosis and management plan to patients and their families; counsel patients on recurrence prevention, including dietary and lifestyle changes; collaborate with a multidisciplinary team for optimal patient care.

topics.title: Benign colon disorder - inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)
objectives: Knowledge: Describe the pathophysiology, epidemiology, and genetic factors contributing to IBD, including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.
Knowledge: Differentiate between Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis based on clinical, endoscopic, radiologic, and histologic features.
Knowledge: Recognize common complications of IBD, including strictures, fistulas, malnutrition, and extra-intestinal manifestations.
Knowledge: Explain the principles of medical and surgical management of IBD.
Knowledge: Discuss the impact of IBD on growth and development in pediatric patients.

History taking: Elicit a focused history from a patient with suspected IBD, including key symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, rectal bleeding, and extra-intestinal manifestations; identify risk factors, including family history, smoking, previous infections, and medication use (e.g., NSAIDs); assess the impact of symptoms on the patient's quality of life, nutrition, and psychological well-being.

Physical examination: Perform a comprehensive abdominal examination, identifying signs suggestive of IBD (e.g., tenderness, mass, distension, perianal disease); recognize systemic signs of IBD, including pallor (anemia), growth failure, clubbing, and extra-intestinal manifestations (e.g., arthritis, erythema nodosum); assess for signs of complications, such as toxic megacolon or perforation.

Differential diagnosis: List and differentiate IBD from other causes of chronic diarrhea and abdominal pain, including infections, celiac disease, irritable bowel syndrome, and malignancy; use clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings to narrow down the differential diagnosis.

Investigations: Identify appropriate laboratory tests, including CBC, CRP, ESR, fecal calprotectin, and stool cultures; interpret endoscopic findings characteristic of IBD; recognize histopathological features of Crohn's disease (granulomas, transmural inflammation) and ulcerative colitis (crypt abscesses, continuous mucosal inflammation); discuss the role of imaging studies such as MR enterography and small bowel ultrasound in diagnosing and monitoring IBD.

Management: Outline the stepwise approach to medical management, including the use of aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, immunomodulators, and biologic therapies; recognize indications for surgical intervention in IBD and describe common surgical procedures; explain the importance of nutritional support, vaccination, and psychological support in managing pediatric IBD.

Communication: Effectively counsel patients and families on the chronic nature of IBD, treatment options, and potential complications; discuss the importance of adherence to treatment and follow-up; provide empathetic communication when discussing prognosis, lifestyle modifications, and coping strategies.

topics.title: Painful limb (limb ischemia & diabetic foot)
objectives: Knowledge: Differentiate between acute and chronic painful limb.
Knowledge: List the causes of acute limb pain.
Knowledge: List the causes of chronic limb pain.
Knowledge: Discuss the holistic approach to assessment of a painful limb.
Knowledge: Discuss the pathophysiology of intermittent claudication, rest pain and tissue loss.
Knowledge: Discuss the difference between embolic versus thrombotic arterial occlusions.
Knowledge: Discuss the possible sources of arterial emboli, and the common sites for embolic occlusions in the body.
Knowledge: Define critical limb ischemia.
Knowledge: Outline the management of acute limb ischemia.
Knowledge: Discuss pathophysiology, risk factors, diagnosis and treatment of DVT including thromboprophylaxis.
Knowledge: Understand the pathology of soft tissue infections, clinical presentation and the principles of management (cellulitis, necrotizing fasciitis).
Knowledge: Discuss the pathophysiology and management options for diabetic foot.

History taking: Differentiate between acute, acute on chronic and chronic limb pain; differentiate between traumatic and non-traumatic causes of limb pain; recognize different types of claudication pain (arterial, venous & neurogenic); elicit symptoms of intermittent claudication & rest pain; determine sites of intermittent arterial claudication including Leriche's syndrome; elicit history of risk factors for developing DVT (bed bound, elderly, visceral malignancy, oral contraceptives, pregnancy, previous DVT, varicose veins); elicit history of diabetes mellitus (age of onset, complications, treatment); elicit drug history (NSAIDs, aspirin, warfarin, OCP); elicit occupational history; elicit personal history such as smoking.

Physical examination: Do a general examination of a patient with painful limb (general status, face expression, gait, deformity); assess vital signs; carry out a comprehensive physical examination (lymphadenopathy, cardiovascular and abdomen); conduct a focused complete limb examination - examining all pertaining systems (skin, arterial, venous, lymphatic, lymph nodes, musculoskeletal, limb measurement for circumference discrepancy, foot deformities, full neurological assessment: sensory, motor, reflexes); demonstrate the technique of palpation of peripheral pulses; demonstrate how to use handheld Doppler to determine different arterial waveforms (triphasic, biphasic & monophasic) compared to venous waveform; demonstrate measurement of ankle brachial pressure indices and discuss their implications; describe an ulcer and recognize gangrene, cellulitis and deformity (discoloration, edema, erythema, tender and crepitus; suspect deeper infections if tenderness is out of proportion and movement of digits is extremely tender); conduct a complete physical examination of the arterial system including pulse identification, auscultation (carotid, renal and femoral bruits), feeling for palpable pulsatile masses, identifying popliteal fossa masses, Doppler evaluation and ankle-brachial pressure index determination; recognize the 6 Ps of acute limb ischemia and signs of acute limb ischemia; recognize signs of chronic limb ischemia (hair loss, thin shiny skin, nail deformity, pallor on elevation, ulceration and gangrene); differentiate between arterial, venous and neuropathic ulcers; differentiate between dry gangrene and infected gangrene; demonstrate examination of venous system (swelling, venous ulcers, features of superficial thrombophlebitis, DVT, varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency); demonstrate examination of lymphatic system (swelling, non-pitting edema, features of lymphatic swelling, elephantiasis, lymph nodes, and superimposed cellulitis); demonstrate how to do measurements of limb swelling and the importance of bony landmarks.
Differential diagnosis: Propose a differential diagnosis for a painful limb (traumatic, inflammatory, and acute versus chronic limb ischemia).

Investigations: Propose appropriate and cost-effective tests e.g. CBC and coagulation profile, inflammatory markers (ESR and CRP), biochemical tests (electrolytes, lactate, LDH), urine and septic workup; ECG, CXR, echocardiography, nerve conduction studies; discuss the order of the diagnostic workup for: acute limb ischemia (U/S, CTA, conventional angiography); chronic limb ischemia (U/S, CTA, MRA, conventional angiography); DVT (ultrasound doppler); propose and discuss the order of diagnostic workup of soft tissue infections (CBC, blood culture, swab culture, x-rays, US, CT, MRI).

Management: Discuss the principles of managing a patient with acute limb ischemia; discuss the interventional and surgical treatment options for patients with acute limb ischemia; discuss the complications associated with prolonged ischemia and revascularization; discuss the complication of myoglobinuria and acute renal failure and how to prevent or treat it; discuss the principles of management of chronic limb ischemia; discuss the endovascular and surgical options in treating patients with chronic limb ischemia; discuss risk of contrast-induced nephropathy and how to prevent it; discuss the indications and different levels of amputations; discuss how to prevent DVT and the principles of treatment; propose a management plan for the care of diabetic foot; propose a management plan for cellulitis and necrotizing fasciitis.

Communication: Elicit history of high-risk behavior, such as smoking, wearing seatbelt, protective measures during sport activities; obtain informed consent for chosen line of management; propose a plan to break bad news to a patient like the need for an amputation.
Attitude: Show empathy while communicating and examining a patient with painful limb; show professionalism in dealing with a patient with painful limb.

topics.title: Scrotal swellings & pain
objectives: Knowledge: Discuss differential diagnosis of acute and chronic scrotal swellings.
Knowledge: Know the common benign and malignant scrotal swellings (solid and cystic scrotal swellings: hydrocele, epididymal cyst, testicular tumors).
Knowledge: Understand that most palpable testicular swellings are malignant in contrast to epididymal masses which are benign.
Knowledge: Discuss commonly used investigations for evaluating scrotal swellings.
Knowledge: Discuss the treatment of different scrotal swellings.
Knowledge: Discuss differential diagnosis of acute scrotal swellings.
Knowledge: Discuss common inflammatory scrotal swellings.
Knowledge: Understand the need for prompt diagnosis and management of testicular torsion.
Knowledge: Discuss commonly used investigations for evaluating acute scrotum.
Knowledge: Discuss the treatment of different painful scrotal swellings and have an overview of the management of acute scrotum (testicular torsion, epididymo-orchitis and varicocele).
Knowledge: Understand how to recognize and evaluate an empty scrotum (testes not palpable).

History taking: Understand that proper history is key to differentiate between scrotal swellings; elicit history of urethral discharge, lower urinary tract symptoms and sexual contact; elicit history of change in size of swelling on standing, lying down and cough.

Physical examination: Appreciate the importance of examining a patient with scrotal/inguinal swellings both lying down and standing; demonstrate how to differentiate between true scrotal swellings and inguinoscrotal swellings; demonstrate how to differentiate between solid and cystic swellings; demonstrate checking for fluctuation and trans-illumination; demonstrate testicular palpation.

Differential diagnosis: Propose differential diagnosis for cystic scrotal swellings; propose differential diagnosis for solid scrotal swellings; differentiate between testicular torsion and epididymo-orchitis.
Investigations: Choose appropriate investigations for a patient with scrotal swelling and pain.

Communication: Elicit sexual history and contact tracing; obtain necessary consent for a patient undergoing scrotal surgery; obtain necessary consent for a patient undergoing surgery for testicular torsion; teach testicular self-examination; spread awareness for early treatment of scrotal conditions.

topics.title: Upper urinary obstruction
objectives: Knowledge: Discuss adaptive response of kidney to distal obstruction.
Knowledge: Discuss the intraluminal, intramural and extraluminal causes of ureteric obstruction.

Knowledge: Discuss commonly used investigations for evaluating upper urinary tract obstruction (ultrasonography, intravenous urography, retrograde pyelography and diuretic renography) and typical findings in congenital obstruction of the pelviureteric junction.
Knowledge: Discuss the usefulness of renogram with frusemide.
Knowledge: Understand the importance of avoiding contrast media and gadolinium in renal failure.
Knowledge: Discuss the treatment of congenital obstruction of pelviureteric junction/vesicoureteric junction.
Knowledge: Discuss management of a patient with an infected obstructed kidney and renal failure and understand that this is a urological emergency.

History taking: Understand that proper history is the key to differentiate between different causes of upper urinary tract obstruction; elicit history of renal/ureteric colic, lower urinary tract symptoms and urinary infection.
Physical examination: Detect renal angle tenderness and dullness; examine for distended urinary bladder.

Differential diagnosis: Differentiate between acute/chronic/unilateral/bilateral/partial/complete obstructions; think of bladder outlet obstruction in case of bilateral upper urinary tract dilatation.

Communication: Counsel patient and family regarding the need for close follow up and early intervention in case of obstructed kidney; counsel patient and family to seek emergency attention if infection develops in presence of obstruction.
Attitude: Understand the importance of ensuring privacy during external genitalia/digital rectal examination and the need for a chaperone during examination.

topics.title: Lower urinary obstruction (bladder outlet obstruction)
objectives: Knowledge: Discuss the common causes of bladder outlet obstruction in male and female.
Knowledge: Explain what LUTS (lower urinary tract symptoms) is, including obstructive and irritative symptoms.
Knowledge: Differentiate between acute and chronic urinary retention and understand the difference in their management.
Knowledge: Discuss the consequences of bladder outlet obstruction.
Knowledge: Discuss the medical and surgical management of bladder outlet obstruction.
Knowledge: Explain the current medical management of BPH.
Knowledge: Explain the mode of action of commonly used medications for BPH.
Knowledge: Discuss the indications for surgical intervention.
Knowledge: Discuss the immediate and late complications of TURP (transurethral resection of prostate).
Knowledge: Understand how to differentiate between BPH and prostate cancer and the importance of PSA (prostate specific antigen).
Knowledge: Define urinary frequency and discuss the three basic causes of urinary frequency (polyuria, bladder instability and reduced bladder compliance).

Knowledge: Discuss the common clinical conditions presenting as urinary frequency (UTI, BPH, diabetes, stones, malignancy, post radiation, diuretics, caffeine, pregnancy, detrusor overactivity, detrusor hyperreflexia, chronic retention).
Knowledge: Understand that pathologies apart from that of the urinary system can present as urinary frequency, like congestive cardiac failure and diabetes insipidus.
Knowledge: Discuss frequency volume chart and evaluation of urinary frequency.
Knowledge: Discuss the medical and surgical therapy of urinary frequency.

History taking: Elicit history of LUTS; elicit past history of sexually transmitted disease, urethral trauma or instrumentation; know the importance of family history of carcinoma prostate; learn the importance of associated symptoms like dysuria, urgency, urinary retention.

Physical examination: Detect palpable bladder; differentiate between acute and chronic retention; examine external genitalia in male and female; do digital rectal examination (DRE) to appreciate anal tone, prostate size and consistency and any rectal mass lesions; check anal tone and perianal sensations to identify neurogenic bladder.

Management: Plan appropriate investigations for a patient presenting with poor stream or urinary retention; interpret uroflowmetry tracing; understand that priority is relief of retention in cases of acute urinary retention before investigations in contrast to chronic retention; do safe urethral Foley catheterization; know the indication for suprapubic catheterization (SPC).
Communication: Importance of eliciting history of co-morbidities and drug intake such as aspirin; importance of informing the patient of retrograde ejaculation while planning TURP.
Attitude: Be compassionate towards patients who are mostly elderly.

topics.title: Hematuria (urology)
objectives: Knowledge: Understand that hematuria is a symptom rather than a disease and that the cornerstone of evaluating a patient with hematuria is a thorough clinical history.
Knowledge: Discuss how hematuria associated symptoms can localize the site and/or cause of hematuria.
Knowledge: List causes of hematuria including systemic diseases that cause blood in urine.
Knowledge: Discuss the symptoms and signs of the most common causes of blood in urine, like genitourinary tract infections, urinary tract stones, trauma and genitourinary tumors.
Knowledge: Discuss the relevant investigations for a patient with hematuria.
Knowledge: Understand the general principles of management of a patient with hematuria.

History-taking skills: Elicit history of associated symptoms like pain abdomen, dysuria, irritative voiding symptoms, passing clots, fever, oliguria, edema, arthritis, rash and weight loss; elicit history of smoking, exercise, medications, diet, bleeding disorder, renal stone disease, travel outside and occupational exposure; establish whether hematuria is initial, terminal or total.
Physical examination: Differentiate between hepatic and renal mass; demonstrate checking for suprapubic dullness and renal angle tenderness.
Differential diagnosis: Understand that painless hematuria and hematuria in patients older than 40 years are more likely to be associated with malignancy.
